PROPOSED TAKEOVER OF HUSKY OIL BY PETRO-CANADA- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. My motion concerns the
pending purchase by Petro-Canada of Husky Oil. This takeover will not add one barrel to Canada's present reserves of oil. It will probably not result in any increased processing of heavy oil which the present owners of Husky Oil would not have undertaken. But it will allow a foreign-owned company to liquidate its Canadian assets and, in the process, make a healthy profit. Husky Oil will not have to reinvest these funds in Canada but will be free to move them out of the country. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That this House deplores this misuse of taxpayer's money by Petro-Canada and urges that the government prohibit it from carrying forward its proposed purchase of Husky Oil.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF DOCUMENT "A TIME FOR ACTION" ON RENEWAL OF CANADIAN FEDERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 41(2), I should like to table a copy, in both official languages, of a document which proposes the principles for the renewal of the Canadian federation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the document I have just tabled before the House of Commons constitutes the first segment of the formal proposals the government wishes to present to parliament and the Canadian people with a view of beginning the renewal of the federation.
The last few months have been a time of deep thought for all Canadians. Within political parties, interest groups, and professional associations, before the Pepin-Robarts Task Force, and in the press, we have attempted to take a new look at our country and its institutions. We have rediscovered its past, sought to understand its present, and tried to envisage its future. We have not yet reached agreement on what Canada should be, but at least we have all agreed that a significant renewal is necessary and that we must sit down to business. [Translation)
The federalism instituted in 1867 and modified to meet our needs over the years has served our country very well. It has involved a largely successful attempt to set up a balanced system based on reason and flexibility and thereby join our communities and regions together in a country blessed with both variety and vigour. Between two orders of loyalty and two levels of government it has established a dynamic equilibrium in which each Canadian could and still can belong in a real and profound way to both his province and his country. It has given Canada the spiritual and physcial strength needed to carve out a place in the world and in history of which we may all feel justly proud.
But Canadian society is still developing. Fortified by the contributions of people from all over the world, it has lost none of its instinctive desire for the new, for the unexplored and for a better life. As a result it now feels cramped within a legal framework devised over one hundred years ago and in an administrative system built piecemeal over the years, and this in turn has given rise to the desire for renewal that is being felt in the country.

The time has come to respond to this desire for renewal among the Canadian people, and it is up to parliament, the federal government, the provincial governments, and all those who hold authority in our society, to ensure that this renewal is carried out promptly, explicitly, and with the greatest respect

for our democratic tradition. Our present uncertainty is not helping the country; it is drawing strength required elsewhere, jeopardizing our economic progress, and eating away at the world community's much-needed confidence in Canada. The federal government therefore urges all Canadians to join it in settling this question without further delay by renewing our federal pact and our sense of belonging to this country. Through this renewal will come the other changes-economic, social, and cultural-to which we are entitled. It is time for action.
The objective of the document I have just tabled is, precisely, to start this process. It sets out the principles of this renewal and their application to the workings of our federal system and the institutions provided for in the constitution. It is no coincidence that it is entitled "A time for Action". It is our firm intention to take concrete measures according to a very specific timetable.
The renewal of the Canadian federation is not the issue of any one political party. It is an issue for all parties to address and to resolve, and the government intends to deal with it in a non-partisan, open-minded manner. We know, Mr. Speaker, that the other parties represented in this House have already done a great deal of work on this issue. Their conclusions regarding the terms and conditions of this renewal may sometimes differ from ours, but their ultimate objectives are probably much the same as ours. We hope, therefore, that we can count on their co-operation in speeding up the process. Let us agree upon the objectives, then we can deal with the terms and conditions, instruments and texts.
We have set ourselves a tight schedule. We therefore urge this parliament, the provincial legislatures and governments, and all Canadians, to begin working with us as soon as possible.

We are placing only two conditions on our proposals for renewal. The first is that Canada continue to be a real federation-that is, a country in which the federal Parliament possesses real powers and the provincial legislative assemblies have powers that are just as real. The second condition is that basic human rights and freedoms be entrenched in the constitution and thus be protected against interference from either order of government. Apart from these prerequisites, we wish to be guided by the will of the citizens who elected us. Our proposals are there to be examined, debated and refined. We are counting on a national consensus to launch the renewal, and we hope that a national consensus will emerge on the nature of this renewal.
"A Time for Action" was not written as an attack on anyone. It was written in support of a cause-that of a renewed Canada geared to our needs. It invites all Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific to define the terms of the Canadian identity, bring our federal system up to date and reshape our constitution in the image of Canada today. As for
June 12, 1978

those who do not share our profound belief that so fundamental a renewal of the Canadian federation is possible, I ask simply that they open their eyes and hearts in all honesty to the desire for change which the great majority of Canadians feel and which "A Time for Action" endeavours to express as faithfully as possible.

Today we are embarking on an important stage in our development, one that will perhaps determine the course of Canada's history. I invite all Canadians to summon their most positive qualities and enter this new stage with enthusiasm, drawing confidence from the very sources of our history. We cannot allow ourselves to miss this unique opportunity to make a collective decision on our future as a country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want at the outset to express my appreciation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for making a copy of both his statement today and the document he has tabled available to me earlier in the day. I must at the same time express a very real concern in that it was only today he sent ministers of his government to communicate the contents of this document directly to the premiers of the provinces, who are the other partners in this confederation. I think that kind of last minute notification of a document of very real importance to the premiers is an indication of the kind of thing that has gone wrong during the last ten years when the federal government, instead of treating the provinces as partners, has treated them as people to be communicated with on matters of real concern to them, only at the last minute.

Hear, hear!
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, some of the proposals contained in this document look strangely familiar. Upon reflection, the Prime Minister will certainly recognize that he is exaggerating when he insists today that we are entering a new era in our development. We believe that that era has started some while ago, and it is high time for the government to catch up. The leader of the government urges all Canadians to think and act. But judging by his proposals, he seems quite content with the appearance of action. We are not much ahead on his true intentions regarding, for instance, certain basic problems such as the distribution of power between the two levels of government.

As I was saying, sir, the Prime Minister calls his document "A Time for Action". I think it would be far more appropriate, judging by its contents, if he called it "A Time for the Appearance of Action". Some of the proposals, I must say, are as interesting now as they were when we first made them.
Hear, hear!

But, sir, the significance of this document is not the presence or the absence of imaginative proposals. What is
The Constitution
significant here is the tone. This document anticipates unilateral changes in a partnership. It distinguishes between two categories of constitutional change: those characterized as phase 1, where there is "full capacity for parliament to act alone", and those characterized as phase II, which "the federal government and the provinces must discuss together . That might be the way to treat an ordinary law, but it is no way at all to approach a constitution. The intention here is quite clear. Where the federal government is obliged to get agreement from the provinces, it will aceept that obligation. Where it has a narrow legal competence to act alone, then it will act alone.
Of course, it pledges consultation in this document in one sentence, but in the next sentence it pledges a deadline thirteen months from now.

The Prime Minister is prompt to praise the virtues of federalism, but he is behaving like the leader of a single type of government. In a federation where the central power and the provinces are to be true partners, the leader of the government has no qualms whatsoever about saying that he intends to proceed unilaterally with some constitutional amendments which are of vital concern to the provinces.

The reason that is particularly alarming is that it has been this very tone, this refusal to regard confederation as a partnership where partners co-operate even when they are not required to, that has done so much damage to our country in this last ten years, on questions ranging last week alone from sales tax to the lottery. That, sir, of course, is a source of partisan disagreement in this House. I do not raise it in a partisan way. There are other times and other topics for partisan division.
I agree with the Prime Minister that this fundamental question is more important than parties, but the fact is that this document fails to reflect, as perhaps sadly its authors failed to recognize, that the paternalistic tone of this proposal is itself a major modern cause for distrust and disunity in Canada. This process, sir, will come to nothing unless that is recognized. Indeed, it may come to worse than nothing because it may deepen the divisions that exist among Canadians. That is particularly true since the reaction of the separatist government of one province is already predictable. That makes it all the more essential that every step is taken to secure a consensus among the other provinces, and that, sir, will happen only if they are treated as full partners in this process and are not faced with deadlines or with declarations that may turn out to impede agreement.
These last two years have shown us all that there is a great deal of agreement in this country about the necessity for constitutional and administrative reform. There is also, as we found as a nation in earlier times of challenge and of crisis, a great deal of good will in Canada that will result in concrete agreement. I found this in Kingston last September when I met with four premiers from one party from very different p: ovinces and secured agreements on important constitutional,

June 12, 1978
The Constitution
administrative, and economic changes. I make the point in passing, sir, that it would be tragic for the unity of this country if we were to deflect attention from the fundamental requirement of this parliament to address ourselves to economic growth over the next six to eight months. I found that kind of agreement also when I discussed those changes arrived at in Kingston with other party leaders in the other provinces in subsequent discussions.
We came to Kingston as partners and we found agreement because there was a basis of mutual respect. The Fathers of Confederation came together as partners, and they found agreement. We can do that again today providing we recognize that confederation is a partnership and not a system where one government can adopt a paternalistic and domineering attitude toward all the others.
There is one other matter of procedure that concerns me in relation to the document that has been tabled here today and the proposal that I understand the Prime Minister is making as to how we proceed with it. That is the role of this parliament. We have demonstrated before in this House of Commons a capacity to secure progress and to secure a consensus on constitutional questions when parliament is given the chance to address those questions. I would hope, sir, that there will be the widest possible role for parliament, not just the government, in considering constitutional and administrative reforms that we must contemplate as a country.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested in his statement today, in recent years Canadians have, indeed, been giving more thought than usual to the problems and prospects of our country. At every level there has been concern that the traditional Canadian dream for a united Canada, committed to a just and exciting society based on liberty and equality for all our people-French-speaking, English-speaking, other ethnic groups, the Inuit, and the Indian-was falling short of realization.

It is ironic and historically sad that this anxiety regarding the future of the country should appear when the Canadians of my generation, whether they are French or English-speaking, have succeeded in gaining unprecedented recognition in the cultural field, and this at the national and international levels. [English]
Beyond this level of creative excitement, Mr. Speaker, as we all know, there have been disturbing and unsettling signs of discontent. It is important that we understand the origins of this discontent. They are to be found in the inequality as it exists between and within our regions. They are to be found in the absence of strong federal leadership which ought to have been positively identifying itself with the cultural excitement of French and English-speaking Canada in recent decades. They are to be found in the absence of federal leadership

which recognizes that the independence of the Canadian economy and all that depends on it are threatened at least as much today by our vigorous neighbours to the south as they were more than 100 years ago, and finally they are to be found in the lack of a specific Canadian constitution which contains in one document guarantees for individual and cultural rights of Canadians as well as a division of responsibilities between federal and provincial authorities.

We must get involved in the political life of our country, show leadership in each of the fields that have a bearing on the country's future, like regional disparities, recognition of fundamental rights or political determination to achieve Canada's economic independence. It is in that perspective that I want to answer today to the Prime Minister's statement.

The highest priority we must set for ourselves is to establish at this time in the hearts and minds of Canadians that we are now embarking upon the development of a future that is both just and exciting, and that deals with all of these questions. Our priority must be to pledge ourselves, not simply to constitutional reform, but, more basically, to the removal of inequalities and the establishment of a viable, healthy, industrial country in this part of North America.
In the broad sense of what our country is about, the document which the Prime Minister has tabled, I regret to say, fails. It is totally devoid of a broad scale of imagination. Regrettably, it deals only with the most general proposals on the constitution and the establishment of linguistic and other rights. As important as these are, they are not new. We all assumed that proposals would be made concerning these areas at some point during this year, and in this sense we accept and support them.
It is worse than regrettable that a document entitled "A Time for Action" is exclusively legalistic in its proposals for the future of our country and of our people. Economic inequalities within our country and the deeply serious matter of the economic viability of our future on the North American continent are virtually ignored. A statement of purpose so narrow in its focus and so devoid of concern for matters beyond a legal framework for our nationhood is totally inadequate to meet our needs as a people at this time.
It is, indeed, time for action. A central concern in the confederation debates more than 100 years ago was the state of the economy of the various provinces. Where is that concern in the document that has been tabled today? The economic position of Atlantic Canada compared to Ontario has worsened since confederation, not improved. We still have millions of people at the poverty level, while the rich still get richer in our country. We have a manufacturing sector which is weaker today than it was a decade ago, and we have more than one million people unemployed. And, as Sir John A. Macdonald would well understand, we cannot stand idly by while our vigorous neighbours to the south daily make inroads on our economic independence as a people. Canadians want action.
June 12, 1978

They want imagination and leadership which will reverse our inequalities and reshape our economy for the requirements of the twentieth century. Legal pedantry of the kind we have today is no substitute for leadership.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for having provided us with a copy of his statement a few minutes before the opening of this sitting. As usual, we were able to read the statements of principles in the newspapers, but we could not be sure if this was improvisation on the part of the reporters or a leak that the government obviously wanted.
The title "A Time for Action" is well chosen because it shows at least that the right hon. Prime Minister has backed down in finally deciding to make an appeal for a real constitution. It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that I did not say a renewed constitution, as the right hon. Prime Minister calls it, because I have always thought that the British North America Act is simply a royal order of the British Crown for its Canadian colony that we have used up to this day. Since it was written in England by the parliament in London, it could not reflect the aspirations of the Fathers of Confederation who had certainly spent many months preparing a thick memorandum for the British government, and this memorandum, which favoured a confederation in which the provinces would have priority, was probably put aside to be replaced by this little private bill which was entitled the British North America Act and which has been the basis for our constitution since 1867.
This is why I agree with the right hon. Prime Minister when he lists certain defects of the present constitution, including the following, and I quote:
It is based largely on acts of the British parliament and has not yet been properly rooted in Canada.
Its provisions are scattered through a large number of statutes, many of which are unknown to the general public.
It has not preamble or statement of principles; its language is obscure, its style plodding and uninspiring.
It has little educative value and Canadians find in it little which inspires patriotism.
It makes no mention of basic rights or freedoms, and it is inadequate to protect language rights.
Its division of legislative powers between the federal and provincial governments is neither as precise nor as functional as might be wished.
And he goes on to enumerate the shortcomings that he finds in the British North America Act. For example, Mr. Speaker, I have always thought that its greatest shortcoming was to have made the federal government the architect with a certain measure of supremacy over the provinces. We reason that very often that is why the federal government instructs the provinces instead of consulting them. Of course, compared to previous agreements the 1867 confederation represented one more step toward Canadian unity, but for many years all the provinces and all Canadians have been hoping for new agreements and their greatest desire would be to see the provinces
The Constitution
initiate consultations within their borders so as to come up with strictly interprovincial conferences, through which they could tell the central government what they expect from it.
We are still convinced that only a confederation including all provinces will bring back harmony in Canada. As long as the federal government interferes in interprovincial conferences to rouse their suspicion and pit them against each other we shall witness the same confusion that has prevailed in the last 110 years in federal-provincial conferences. We should recognize once for all that the provinces will have the final veto.
So, if the federal government really wants to do something useful for Canada it should encourage the provinces to get together and agree on a constitution. Shall we have a true confederation under our new constitution? This is the first question. Or will it be a federation as the present government sees it, that is to say a profitable federalism with a strong central government and in which the provinces will be nothing more than administrative districts.
I think the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) best expressed the thoughts of the government when he declared in the House recently that the ideal solution for Canada would be a single government! With such statements, Mr. Speaker, this is something we will have to consider because if we are to judge someone through his actions, the ten years of administration of the present government are not very favourable to provincial autonomy. The many intrusions into provincial jurisdictions and the Quebec jurisdiction particularly make Quebeckers wonder about their future.
This is why I ask the government to avoid any confrontation at least with Quebec, end personal conflicts and try negotiation. We must absolutely avoid the unfortunate mistake of 1867. We must absolutely avoid it and judging from the orientation of this issue, I think that we are going towards even more centralization in which the federal government will have almost all powers and will leave only secondary powers to the provinces. I sound a warning note to the right hon. Prime Minister and all government members and I hope we will change our orientation so as to favour the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I have been trying to obtain a copy of this document. It has gone to my office. This has not been very helpful to me in posing any questions I might have to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-
We are all in the same boat.

I do not know why my friend over there is so sensitive. I understand what the Prime Minister said in his comments. This document is of some importance, and I understand he will accept questions in relation to it. It is perhaps a good time to get enlightenment-

June 12, 1978
The Constitution
There it is!
Thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct several questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to this document which is long on generalizations and pretty short on specifics.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister, for example, some specific questions with regard to certain proposals which are included. He said in his statement and in the document that he would like to invite all Canadians to participate in the discussion on constitutional change-constitutional renewal. I am interested in the forum that would be provided for this. The Prime Minister will remember that last year about this time we on this side of the House proposed that a joint parliamentary committee be set up to provide that forum wherein all Canadians could participate and make their views known with regard to constitutional review. That suggestion was not accepted at that time; it was bypassed by the Pepin-Robarts commission. I know that later this year with the constitutional conference, by necessity parliament will again be bypassed.
I make a special plea to the Prime Minister this afternoon to consider referring this document immediately-and he might inform us on this point-and I would ask him how detailed proposals will be presented. Will they be presented to parliament by way of legislation? If so, will he refer this document with any legislation forthcoming before the end of this session to a special joint parliamentary committee which would sit throughout the summer months to study these proposals and allow Canadians to appear before it to make their views known, so that parliament indeed can have a role in the renewal of our constitution?

Mr. Speaker, it would be our intention to propose the setting up of such a joint parliamentary committee. Before the end of the month we would like to find a day, or perhaps two, on which to have a debate on the government proposals, with a view to setting up such a committee at the end of the debate. I am sure that all parties in the House will be discussing an appropriate committee and appropriate timing for such a debate.

I take it by that that the Prime Minister will also consider the suggestion that a special parliamentary committee be appointed at least before the end of the month to sit through the summer and have input into these proposals later in the year.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister to tell us as well the status of the Pepin-Robarts commission in relation to the proposals being put forward. Would the Prime Minister say whether these proposals are coming forward by way of legislation before the end of the month, and would he also indicate the particular status of the Pepin-Robarts commission at this point, a commission which was appointed on July 5 last year with a mandate initially for one year, which was to provide a

source of advice to the government on unity issues? That commission has not yet issued a report and it is not anticipated that its report will be forthcoming for some months. What is going to happen to that report? Will it be superseded by proposals that the government puts forward, and where does it stand in relation to the government's proposals?

Mr. Speaker, when the Pepin-Robarts commission was set up, as the hon. lady reminds us correctly, it was intended to report within a year. Then when it was apparent the number of presentations on the task of the commission was such that it would not be able to report finally before the end of the year, it was expected that perhaps there might be an interim report which the government could have consulted before bringing down this particular white paper. We understand that that has not been possible. Therefore, we had to proceed with this white paper without the benefit of the Pepin-Robarts commission report.
I would point out that the proposals of the government at this stage, though they are a white paper and do represent government policy, are in front of parliament and the country for the purposes of discussion. As it is stated in this particular paper, Mr. Speaker, we do expect a federal-provincial conference on the constitution early in the fall. We hope that there too there will be a possibility of input from the provinces. So we would have many sources of input, the standing committee, which the hon. lady mentioned, the Pepin-Robarts committee, reactions from the country of course, and finally the federal-provincial conference of first ministers. As a result of all that, after having heard from everyone, the provincial governments, the House of Commons, and the people of Canada, we would then propose to proceed in the House of Commons in the next session with a bill for adoption, as it is said in the white paper, before July 1, 1979.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure from what the Prime Minister has said and what this document states that they are one and the same thing, for example, "the government will soon be informing parliament and all Canadians of its details." I still do not know whether or not the Prime Minister intends to introduce those details by way of legislation or by way of a further white paper, because there is very little in the way of detail here as to the specifics of any of the proposals. Surely we would need more to go on than this? The government goes on to say, "There is no expectation that these proposals will be passed by parliament without change." So, unless we know something of the detail of the proposals, it is very difficult to formulate any views on them or to suggest changes. These are very broad measures indeed. I would like to know whether it is the government's intention to introduce those details before the end of the month.

Mr. Speaker, the government intends to proceed in two stages on the white paper tabled today, and which is the object of today's discussion. It intends to put forward the general principles on Canadian identity, and the principles for renewal, the way in which we want to renew the practice of federalism. We did hope that this would cause some reflection
June 12, 1978

in parliament, and outside, on the principles which inspire government's actions. This will be followed before the end of the month by a bill which will be given first reading in this Elouse. It is on that bill that we intend to have the House leaders look for the possibility of debate for the setting up of a standing committee, a special committee of the House of Commons and of the Senate, or two special committees, if this is what is preferred by members of parliament of both Houses, so that they will be able to take cognizance of the bill, not after second reading; the bill itself, or the subject matter will be referred to the committees, Mr. Speaker.
I must say the first reading of that bill does give me some concern now. Having heard from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) that we must first consult with the provinces before doing anything here, I am wonderig if we should show the bill to the premiers before showing it to the House of Commons. This would cause me some concern, but if that is the view of the Leader of the Opposition, of course we would be prepared to do that.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Shallow and wrong again.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister concerning some detail. I have read in the white paper, and I have heard the Prime Minister say, that we will get some details later on. One particular matter of interest to me and on which perhaps he could shed some light concerns the Senate, to be renamed the House of Federation. Could the Prime Minister tell us now what the government has in mind in terms of appointment by the provinces? Just what kind of detail has the government already worked out on that subject matter?

Mr. Speaker, this would be spelled out in very considerable detail in the bill which will be given first reading in the House. In this white paper, I repeat, we have intended to state the principles, the general lines of action, but the details will be contained in the bill.

Mr. Speaker, just on the question of principle which is outlined in the white paper, the stated intention of the government is by means of reforming the Senate to give the provinces a greater and more effective say in Ottawa. I would like to ask the Prime Minister, considering there is no talk about changing the power of the Senate-thank God- will this whole operation not be a bit hollow because what is being proposed is to give the provinces authority in a body that quite appropriately has no power in Ottawa?

Mr. Speaker, we hope that is the very subject which will be discussed by the country and by the joint committee of the House of Commons and of the Senate. The hon. member, without benefit of seeing the proposals, suggested that it might be quite hollow. I hope that we will benefit from his intellectual resources when we come to discuss this proposition. He realizes, of course, that in a parliamentary system there is a choice to be made by those who are writing the constitution between having a second chmber which is truly representative of the people of the regions or provinces,-
The Constitution
which presumably would be elected with all the attendent problems of cabinet and responsible government,-or having some other form of representation. We come down on one side of the choice, but I am sure we will benefit from the insight of the hon. member into this problem.

Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister confirm for us that when the bill is brought forward, pertaining to the Senate particularly, the government will not be imposing an increase in the powers of the Senate?

Mr. Speaker, I think in order to avoid answering in detail any of these questions, I must ask the hon. member to be patient and to wait until the bill comes forward. He will see what powers we propose for the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, on page 11 of the document there is a phrase which reads as follows:
The courts... .conferred on the federal authority most of the powers necessary for the government of the federation as a whole.
That referred to a process. I am wondering if it is an accurate interpretation of that particular section. It is on page 11, about two-thirds of the way down. I am sorry, I do not have the original copy. I will give the quotation again.
I have it.

Does the government intend by that to indicate its view that the federal government does not now have all of the authority that it requires, and all of the powers necessary for the government of the federation as a whole? If that is the case, can the Prime Minister indicate to us what kinds of new powers he thinks are necessary to be added to the central authority?

Mr. Speaker, this paragraph in reality refers to the historical evolution. 1 think it is generally recognized that the Canadian federation today is less centralized in practice than it was 110 years ago, although there has been that great redistribution of powers. That is all this particular paragraph intends.
In so far as the distribution of powers in a new federation is concerned, which seems to be of interest to the Leader of the Opposition, we do intend and do say that this is open for discussion. We are ready for a re-examination of the functions of both levels of government and a redistribution of powers in whatever way is of greatest utility to the citizen. However, no suggestion is made that it should result in a greater decentralization or, indeed, in a greater centralization. We think there should be some shifts of power in both directions.
I would certainly incur the wrath of the Leader of the Opposition if I were to indicate now without the benefit of consultation, what we would like to see become federal jurisdiction which is now provincial jurisdiction.

Oh, oh!
6292

June 12, 1978
The Constitution

I am quite sincere. The Leader of the Opposition does present me with a dilemma. I repeat it to him. Would he like us to show the premiers the bill before we show it to the House of Commons? I am in his hands and will do whatever he suggests is best.

Mr. Speaker, I rather think the Prime Minister is anticipating himself by four or five months by putting questions to me, but I will be delighted to answer them. I think it would be very profitable for the system if the Prime Minister were to get together with his counterparts in the provinces and have some kind of discussion now which might serve as the basis for proposals that might come from the federal government or from the provinces. This business of people issuing manifestos from behind their jurisdictional barricades will not take us very far. I hope the Prime Minister might follow the example that I set for him, since he has raised this question, when I met with the premiers at Kingston. I wonder if I might now ask the Prime Minister this, just for the purpose of clarification. On page 23 the document states that the government will therefore be putting forward proposals regarding constitutional provisions for certain institutions of the executive of the central government. Can the Prime Minister tell me in a general way what that phrase means?

Mr. Speaker, in his comments on consultation the Leader of the Opposition makes bold that he met four premiers. I must remind him that throughout the months of November and December I met every one of the premiers and we had lengthy discussions on the constitution and economic matters. In those discussions I spoke at great length about the subject matter of this white paper. I indicated to them that we were proceeding with phase I and phase II, and asked what they thought about it. I indicated in phase I what it was our intention to discuss.
I not only had these discussions with the premiers, but the hon. member will know that there were many speeches and comments made by the premiers either resulting from or following upon those discussions, and we do have the benefit of the views of many, if not all, of those premiers on the constitution.
I will be tabling later this week, when my letters have been received by the premiers, a lengthy letter which is in their hands at this moment on the white paper, and commenting on some of the proposals which they have made on constitutional change in the past months.
We must consider that for something like 52 years this subject of constitutional renewal has been debated in parliament after parliament. It was debated during several provincial conferences between 1968 and 1971, and was the subject of consultation time and time again since then at meetings of the premiers and with myself on the constitution.
I think the House will recognize that at some point it is not only natural but desirable for the government to give leadership and to say that, after all these consultations, this is what we think. However, we are of course anxious to know what the opposition thinks and what the premiers think. That is why

this very day and in the following days of this week there will be meetings with the premiers on the basis of this paper and on the basis of the general content of the bill.
When we do table the bill in this House, before the end of the month, I hope we will not hear from the Leader of the Opposition that it is full of platitudes and, to use his expression, deja vu, a lot of things that have just been rehashed and, on the other hand, objecting that it has not been shown to the provinces in advance. This is just a general comment which I mean to be helpful to the hon. Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister was so overcome by the privilege of putting a question that he forgot to answer the one I put. I am sure he would like to redirect his attention to the meaning of the proposal for certain institutions. To save the time of the House, will he also indicate just how firm is the timetable of July 1, 1979?

Mr. Speaker, the reason why I made a lengthy answer is because the Leader of the Opposition always brings in preambles when he makes suggestions. I think it is normal that I make some comment on them.
In terms of his particular question on the executive, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition probably knows that in the present BNA Act the function of the executive and its composition are not spelled out in any detail. It would be our intention in the bill presented to the House of Commons to spell them out in quite a bit of detail.
On the second question, Mr. Speaker, that of the dealine, we think that within the next 12 months and 19 days it is reasonable for the country and parliament to be able to make up their mind on what the federal government, acting alone under the constitution, can do.
I repeat what I said in my statement some minutes ago. We hope this will be approached in a non-partisan spirit. Many of the proposals we have made and will make find their echo in proposls made on the other side of the House in their policy paper on the constitution. Indeed, many of the provincial premiers have been saying things which will find an echo in our bill.
In having the benefit of the bill very soon, and having it before them until the federal-provincial conference in the fall, we hope the premiers will be able to express some concrete response to this in so far as we are anxious to have their opinions, even in areas where the federal government and parliament can act alone. We hope this will be true of the Leader of the Opposition, and his party as well, and that between now and the next four months he will be able to arrive at some view on what the federal institutions and federal parliament are, and how the federal institutions and parliament should be composed in order to respond more accurately to the aspirations of the Canadian people and the principles set out in this white paper, assuming that these principles of renewal are some with which the opposition can agree. If they are not, we are once again prepared to discuss these principles and modify them for the better.
June 12, 1978

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. There are some ten or more members standing to put questions at this time. The Chair is expected to exercise a discretion about the duration of this kind of question period. It is certainly far too soon now to consider stopping it. I do not mean that. Neither do I think it is intended that these question periods after a statement afford the opportunity for an exhaustive discussion on any subject on any particular day. Perhaps I could recognize a few more hon. members, but I shall have to ask that the questions be kept brief.

I know Your Honour will not lose sight of the fact that we are dealing with an important document in the history of our country and one which conceivably has implications for the future. The background to my question is a study taking place in Toronto today at which provincial ministers of urban affairs and housing are meeting with the federal minister to discuss his clumsy intrusion into provincial affairs. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already dissociated himself from the remarks made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellett) who stated at the conference of the Canadian Federation of Mayors in Edmonton last week that the role of the municipalities must be fully enshrined in the constitution as an additional level of government on its own. As I say, the Prime Minister has dissociated himself from that statement, but perhaps he will explain what the intentions of the government are in this area. The right hon. gentleman talks about the trend to urbanization and growth of our cities; he suggests the population of some of them might be greater than that of certain provinces, and talks about Canadian cities as being a new problem which will require attention. When considering such cities, is he thinking about bringing in mayors and municipalities within a constitutional context?

Mr. Speaker, I suggest the hon. gentleman is confusing two areas of discussion. To the extent that the quotation he gave refers to something said in this debate, what we are saying is that when Canada was founded 110 years ago the Fathers of Confederation were dealing with a largely rural society, whereas today the majority of Canadians live in cities. This has created not only a new power relationship but a great many new problems, and it is necessary to deal with them. As to the principles which the government has in mind, I would refer to chapter IV on renewing the practice of federalism, and particularly to page 17 where a certain number of proposals for action are set out.
We have made two proposals in particular-I shall not take up the time of the House reading them but they are there on page 17 and their intention is, to eliminate wasteful duplication where it exists by attempting, along with the provinces, to define more accurately the areas where the provinces and the federal government should be acting each in its own sphere. We will be making special proposals to the provinces for action in this area. When problems, by their very nature, come under shared or joint jurisdictin we will also make proposals to ensure that this joint jurisdiction is exercised jointly and in
The Constitution
consultation. I commend page 17 to the attention of the hon. member.

I refer again to the statement made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs at the meeting of the Canadian Association of Mayors in Edmonton when according to newspaper reports:
. .. Mr. Ouellet assured the delegates their municipalities would be full and equal partners with the other levels of government in current discussions on constitutional reforms.
Given the constitutional fact of life that the cities are creatures of the provinces, an aspect of jurisdiction which the provinces jealously guard, would the Prime Minister tell the House how the government intends to go about bringing the municipalities in on this so-called constitutional reform? Does he envisage, for example, a constitutional conference which would include the provinces and the municiaplities?

We think, Mr. Speaker, that the municipalities do have a role in being a voice of the people at the administrative level where they exist and we hope that many of them will be heard not only by the government but by the joint parliamentary committee which we propose to set up. Indeed, I believe the Pepin-Robarts committee has heard from many representatives of municipalities who have their views on the constitution. We would not propose by any narrow legalism- to borrow a phrase from the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent)-to silence them and say they should not express views on a new constitution.
Will they be at the constitutional conference or not? That is the question. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs has indicated clearly that they would be consulted.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I repeat: they will be consulted.

Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that the government intends to move in two stages. I would like to ask a short question about each stage. I understand that in the first stage legislation will be brought down shortly to deal with those matters which come solely under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I want to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if that includes the basic human rights to which he referred in his statement a short time ago or, in view of the fact that provincial governments have some voice in certain matters pertaining to human rights, whether this will be left until the second stage? Can we expect, in the legislation which is to be introduced later this month, clarification of the government's position with respect to basic human rights?

Yes, I think the question is very important and I shall attempt to answer it, first in general and then in particular. In general, Mr. Speaker, we all know there are some areas under the BNA Act-the Constitution of Canada-in which the federal government can act alone. There are other areas where the provinces can act alone. Then there are areas where the two levels must act together and, again, there
80045-31)4

June 12, 1978
The Constitution
are areas where they can act together but each in their own sphere. The bill of rights is in this fourth category. We intend bringing in a bill of rights indicating that parliament would be bound by it as a constitutional document. We realize that certain applications of a bill of rights cannot be binding on the provinces in the sense that they raise the matter of provincial jurisdiction. In these particular areas we hope that the provinces would want to be bound by the bill of rights. In other words, there would be a provision for opting in by the provinces, by concurrent legislation, by joint resolution or whatever the formula might be, into a bill of rights which we hope would eventually bind all Canadians.

I thank the Prime Minister for that answer. The second question I want to ask is with respect to phase II, which involves discussions between the federal and provincial governments. Having regard to the division of powers, particularly with respect to Sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act and the amending formula, which is probably the most difficult part of all, and was certainly the rock upon which the Victoria charter foundered, I ask the Prime Minister this: what is to be the modus operandi which the government has in mind? Is a white paper to be prepared which will be submitted to the provinces, following which meetings will be held? Or will meetings be held first? Is the government intending to have some discussion in parliament or by a committee of parliament with regard to what the government has in mind, always recognizing that there might be changes as a result of negotiations with the provinces? Just what are the procedures which the government has in mind?

Mr. Speaker, with respect, might I slightly correct the preamble to the hon. member's question? It was not on the amending formula that the Victoria conference foundered, to use his expression. It was on something else. I believe there was general agreement at the Victoria conference, including the province of Quebec, on the amending formula. As I said in my letters to the premiers over the past years, we would hope that this formula would still serve us as a basis for patriating the constitution. What we intend to do in the course of the summer is to publish a document which would bring this subject to the attention of Canadians at large, as this white paper has done, and which would go into the various possibilities of amending formulas which historically have made some progress in Canada, and give rise to discussion among Canadians, in this House, in the legislatures and elsewhere, on this subject.
At the federal-provincial conference in the fall we would like to deal with the matter of patriation and amendment but we do realize that, strictly speaking, this could be considered outside the area of what we call phase I, since it does call for provincial consent. We do hope, however, that enough progress will be made on this matter so that we would be able to proceed by July 1 of next year not only with matters of federal jurisdiction but perhaps in a certain number of areas such as the bill of rights and the amending formula on which progress

could also be made. But we realize that on this we cannot act unilaterally and we hope there will be co-operation from provincial governments, which we think will be forthcoming if the opposition parties share our views on some of these matters, and that is why we intend to present it to parliament in as non-partisan a fashion as possible.

Mr. Speaker, following up on the questions put by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), the paper tabled today by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announces, for the implementation of the proposals contemplated in phase two of the constitutional reform, the promulgation of a new constitution for July 1, 1981. However, the paper does not seem to provide for any specific mechanism for federal-provincial negotiations such as that, for example, which was established to pave the way for the Victoria conference. It does not provide either for any process of popular identification with that effort to Canadianize our institutions. Nor does it specify whether a popular sanction is being contemplated by way of a referendum on that new constitution. Has the Prime Minister made provisions for a way of breaking the vicious circle of distrust and disillusionment that has set in the minds of Canadians since the failure of the Victoria conference with respect to the federal or provincial governments claiming the monopoly on good intentions in the area of constitutional proposals and what does he intend to do to associate as many Canadians as possible to that long awaited reform so it will best reflect the Canadian reality and that consensus the Prime Minister was referring to in his remarks will not be an illusory one and will not feed the frustration felt by many Canadians?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is perfectly right. That mechanism is not provided for in the white paper that we just tabled before the House but we intend to take precisely that problem before the House of Commons, before that joint committee of the House and the Senate and also at the premiers' meeting in the fall. There are certainly several sections under which the government could approach that problem, and the hon. member referred to some of those means. Before setting the final form we prefer to take the matter before the House and before the premiers.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the statement in the document that the draft bill, which 1 assume will be introduced later this month, will obviously not be an item which will be passed directly without change, and the subsequent consultation that will take place this fall with the provinces, I wonder if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can indicate if there is to be some sort of deadline to be applied to
June 12, 1978

the provinces with respect to the consultation that will take place on phase I. In what way will the recommendations which come forward from some kind of meeting between the Prime Minister and his provincial counterparts come before this special joint committee so that they can be fully considered before a final bill is presented to parliament, particularly given the deadline that the Prime Minister has enunciated?

What we will table before the House of Commons is a bill for first reading. This is frequently done, as the House knows, so that there can be discussion on the basis of that bill. I have indicated that, following the committee report and following the federal-provincial conference, the government will be prepared in the next session of parliament to introduce a bill for first reading and adoption by the House. It is precisely because we want to make sure that we will meet the deadline of July 1 next year that we will attempt in the bill before the House to meet, as much as possible, the concerns expressed by the provinces, by the many parties in the House, and by the Canadian people, as regards the precise reforms that we are putting before the House. It is possible that on some of the proposals we are making we will find a better formula, and although the bill represents government policy to which we are all bound, we make it quite clear in the white paper that changes can be made to the bill between the form in which it is first presented and its form in the next session.

It is difficult to talk about a bill which is not before us, but I wonder to what degree the provinces will be able to make suggestions, perhaps fundamental suggestions, about the nature of the specifics that are in this draft bill, because I think that to some degree it circumscribes the fundamental consultation which takes place with the provinces. I suppose that the subsequent question then is: when those recommendations come to the committee and the committee makes its own recommendations, will there be any further consultations with the provinces before the government brings forward, as the Prime Minister said, its final bill for first reading in the next parliament?
The hon. member asks to what degree there will be consultation with the provinces.
No, the extent of change.

They will be given the bill and they will be present at the first ministers' conference in the autumn. We are anxious to improve the bill in any way that can be suggested by the provinces or by the parliamentary committee. I would just remind the hon. member that the very nature of this bill-subject of course to the provisions which I pointed out to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), some of which will call for provincial consent if they are going to be bound by it-will be to act in areas under federal jurisdiction.
We believe that after weeks and months of consultation parliament must make up its mind at some point. I am not saying that should be in November, December, January or March; I am just saying that at some point we hope that the bill, presented in the next session of parliament, will reflect the
The Constitution
collective wisdom of the government, of the opposition parties, and of the premiers of every province. But we are all realistic enough to know that it is unlikely that we will get every province to agree with the proposals for change that we are making. We already know from a press conference on Friday that at least one province, without having even seen the white paper, has decided that it is no good. So I cannot say that we will only proceed with the bill when everybody is agreed. 1 do hope that we will have established a large measure of consensus across the country, and particularly on all sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already alluded to the fact that a constitutional document is a political document in the best sense of the word and will require all parliamentary co-operation between the parties. I realize that there are two sides to every coin, but considering the fact that most of the members from the province of Quebec are sitting on the government side and, as everybody knows, most members from the west are on this side of the House, would it not have been wiser to constitute an all-party committee of the House before a bill of any kind was presented? I put that forward as a proposition. For example, I feel I might go to a committee where a bill has been presented and, although the government says it has read our party's proposals, where I will not feel there has been individual input. Would it not be wiser, I ask the Prime Minister, in view of what I said, to constitute an all-party parliamentary committee before we are faced with bills of any kind, even though we are only dealing with exclusively federal jurisdiction?

1 must point out to the hon. member that this debate has been going on for quite a number of years, and I think that by now most of us have made up our minds generally on the way in which we think a new constitution should be oriented. The opposition party has published a policy paper indicating how they think the constitution should be reformed. As I said earlier, the government has benefited from this policy paper, much as we have benefited from the policy paper put out by the government of Ontario, from the western policy conference, and from statements made by various premiers across the land. 1 would remind the hon. member that there was such a committee which sat and which reported in 1972. The conclusions of that committee inspired us in drafting this document and in drafting the bill which will be put before the House.
At some point the hon. member must realize that it is up to someone to make up his mind and say, "This is what we think corresponds to the best interests of the country at this time and for a long period to come". This is what the bill will be. I know the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) well enough to know that he will not be inhibited merely because a bill is there for first reading only. I am sure he will continue to ensure that the government benefits from his wise thoughts in constitutional matters.

June 12, 1978
The Constitution

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to the statement of principle entitled: "Pre-eminence of citizens and of their freedoms". In part the principle reads:
The renewal of the federation must confirm the pre-eminence of citizens over institutions, guarantee their rights and freedoms, and ensure that these rights and freedoms are inalienable.
On a number of occasions this afternoon the Prime Minister spoke about leadership on the part of the federal government which he now leads. Is it his intention, in a non-partisan way, to bring forward amendments in respect of more odious provisions of such legislation, bills, and acts, as the Official Secrets Act and the War Measures Act? Some time ago the Prime Minister promised drastic changes in this regard. I wonder if he can give the leadership which he talks about in the area over which he and his government have exclusive jurisdiction, and indicate that immediate and dramatic steps will be taken to show where the government stands on this very important principle.

Mr. Speaker. I think the answer is contained in the knowledge we all have now of the present Canadian Bill of Rights. As we know, it is an act of federal parliament which is variously interpreted by the courts. I remind the hon. member that the Bill of Rights, brought in by the former leader of the Conservative party, makes an exception for the War Measures Act, and has provisions for the War Measures Act overriding normal acts of parliament. In the bill we bring forward, it is our intention to make sure that the Bill of Rights, as stated in the constitution, will have precedence over every and all bills of the House of Commons. That can apply to any bill to which the hon. member wants to refer.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept the answer of the Prime Minister as far as it goes, but he has avoided and or neglected answering my specific question concerning his intentions in respect of the Official Secrets Act and the War Measures Act. Will he in fact demonstrate the good faith and the position the government takes in that connection?
The final part of my supplementary question is in respect of the entire question of freedom of information which is receiving some consideration now. In that regard, according to the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) and the government, the question which is causing concern within cabinet is whether the government will accept the proposition, as far as freedom of information is concerned, that the arbitration of the rights of Canadians will be one which is binding upon the government, notwithstanding the fact that the argument often used is that our parliamentary system is based on British tradition. Will he give us the assurance he is committed to the idea that whoever is to be the final arbiter, judicial or otherwise, the final arbiter will have the power to bind the institution of government and the cabinet in particular?

Mr. Speaker, with respect, 1 think we are beginning to deviate from the subject matter of this white paper. I want to assure the hon. member that legislation will be before his eyes very soon, before the end of the month. He

can read the sections on the Bill of Rights and fundamental guarantees. If he wants to propose some amendment, assuming the thought is not already there, to make the constitution supreme over the War Measures Act, or over the practices of cabinet secrecy and other such practices, I hope he feels free to move such an amendment.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister whether according to the white paper, it is considered that the guarantee of linguistic equality suffices to establish the equality of the two founding nations. For instance, if we want to go further in that field, will the reform of the Supreme Court allow for the addition of a court, which might be called constitutional, where the Anglophones and Francophones of Canada would be represented equally? Finally, Mr. Speaker, still with a view to Canadianizing our institutions, is the government at this point willing to call in question again, or at the very least to reassess, our ties with the British Crown?

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the first question 1 must, regretfully, give the hon. member the same type of answer that I gave hon. members on all sides of the House, namely that at this stage I do not want to give the details of the specific provisions dealing with the supreme court in the bill we shall soon introduce in the House. As for the second question, Mr. Speaker, I can say to the hon. member that we intend to reaffirm the fact that the Canadian Constitution is a constitution that sets up a constitutional monarchy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I note there are other hon. members who wish to ask questions. Certainly I think time ought to be taken for them. In light of the time already spent, I think questions should be confined to those members who have been present throughout the discussion and have sought the floor to ask questions. As I have noted, those members are: the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau).

Mr. Speaker, perhaps my question will appear to be somewhat naive, but perhaps the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) can indicate his views on this. Is it his intention to have this parliament deal with the first phase of this program?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, my question is closely related to the one just asked. On page 25 of the white paper I notice the government pledges itself to seek passage of such constitutional legislation before July 1, 1979. Specifically I notice the following words: "pledges itself to seek passage".
June 12, 1978

Given the life of this parliament which, according to my understanding, will end on July 8 or 9, 1979, this particular legislation will have had to pass this House by May 8 or 9, 1979. In other words, some 11 months hence. Is that the understanding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)?

Mr. Speaker, certainly the hon. member is mistaken when he talks about a date in May. Hopefully the date in July will permit us to proceed before the House of Commons well into the spring. I am sure there are other constitutional experts, but I hope we will not have to do this on the eve of July 1. I hope that well before winter is out parties will have made up their minds on what is best in terms of constitutional reform, and that they would be prepared to vote on it.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister deliberately misunderstood my question.
My other derives from comments which appear on page 24 of the white paper. I am referring to the amending procedure and the patriation. Recognizing as the white paper does that many of the propositions will have to be passed by the House of Commons in London, I come down to the form. The Prime Minister has talked about a bill. In effect, is he talking about bills or resolutions which will be forwarded to London for passage, including such things as the amending process and certain other features? Even the division of powers under our existing constitution, prior to the constitution being patriated, might well have to be approved, at least in substance, in London. How does the Prime Minister plan to proceed in this particular matter? Will it be by bill which would be something we would enact in this House? Will it be by resolution which would be forwarded to Westminster for sanction?

In the case of the measure that will be presented to the House before the end of the month, it is quite clearly a bill in the normal and regular form. Other steps such as patriation can and might be taken by way of joint resolution of both Houses, but that is not for debate at this particular phase now. We are talking of a bill which will be tabled before this House before the end of the month.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief question which I think is of importance to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Recently I had the opportunity of meeting with the National Indian Brotherhood and with the Indian chiefs of Saskatchewan. They were concerned that the treaty rights of the Indian people be enshrined in any new constitution. I am wondering whether the Prime Minister is contemplating enshrining the treaty rights of the Indians in the constitution, as well as the rights of the Inuit people of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, we will make quite sure in the bill we want to present, and in any further action, that any rights enjoyed by the Indian and native people, the Inuit, will not be taken from them but, on the contrary, will be protected.
The Constitution
Mr. Speaker, I assume it can also be taken that the Indian people will be consulted before the bill is finally passed?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, and I would hope that the parliamentary committee would see its way clear, particularly in that area, to consult these groups.

During the weekend, it has been said that, according to the white paper which has been tabled, the federal government was not thinking of dropping any of its powers. Would the Prime Minister specify that this allegation is false and that the federal government intends to consider the abandonment of some of its powers, and perhaps to reshuffle the federal powers in a way which would be favourable to the federal government? Also, in this redistribution of powers, is the Prime Minister considering only a transfer of powers from the federal government to the provincial governments or vice versa or does he intend to give some importance to regional governments?

Mr. Speaker, the government's proposal to that effect is clear. On the basis of the two basic principles, which consist in the preservation of a true federation and in the protection of individual rights, we say that everything can be a matter of negotiation. So it is clear that in the area of the sharing of powers, we are prepared to discuss the transfer of powers in one way or the other so that the result would be more appropriate, functionally speaking, to the necessity of a better government.
In answer to the second question, Mr. Speaker, I would say that at the present stage of our proposals, we have not yet entered the area of the detailed distribution of powers and consequently, we cannot answer the hon. member's question immediately, but we wish to have in-depth discussions with the provinces in order to have their points of view on that issue.

Mr. Speaker, I noted some remarks made by the right hon. Prime Minister a moment ago, and what worries me a little is the importance that was given to the Pepin-Robarts commission. Last year, the Prime Minister had announced with much emphasis the creation of that commission and I think that all Canadians expected a lot from that group of experts. We realize that the commission may not have been able to make its report within the prescribed delay, but how can the right hon. gentleman explain to the Canadian people that, given those delays, he has decided himself to write this document which in fact repeats many comments he has already made to us, with the only difference that he put them on paper? I think that the Canadian people expected very much from that report and we had reason to believe that it would help parliament make the new legislation that the Prime Minister intends to submit. Does the Prime Minister really

June 12, 1978
The Constitution
intend to present his draft legislation before the report of the commission?

Mr. Speaker, as many other hon. members, the hon. member pestered me with questions to know when we were going to table our constitutional proposals. We have just tabled them. I indicated earlier, in answer to his leader, that of course we would have liked to have the views of the Pepin-Robarts commission before tabling this first project, but I explained that it was not possible. The Pepin-Robarts commission had too much work, many more consultations than expected at first; this session will close at the end of the month and we think that the country and the opposition in particular would have a right to complain if we had not tabled our proposals before the Pepin-Robarts commission tabled their own, either in late fall or in midwinter. So we decided to go ahead on our own but, as I explained earlier, during the next session of parliament we will introduce a new bill which will take into consideration not only the views of all hon. members, but also resolutions from the Pepin-Robarts commission.

Mr. Speaker, does the right hon. Prime Minister understand my question? He must recognize that his statement is extremely serious as concerns the cost of this commission for Canadians. I think that, like all members of the House, he recognizes the great value of the members of the commission and the importance that it has had. Now, the right hon. Prime Minister finds it very easy to say: Well, they did not have time to submit their report so I have decided to write a book which should be entitled "The Future Canadian Constitution".
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that my colleagues have comments to make on this issue, but Canadians have given great importance to this report, Mr. Robarts and Mr. Pepin have stated how important it is to submit their report, we await with great anticipation the report of this commission, and I do not think that the right hon. Prime Minister can ignore this report to introduce constitutional reforms. I would be very insulted if I were a member of this commission. I therefore ask the right hon. Prime Minister to at least attempt to obtain the report of the commission so that the House of Commons can discuss this issue on the basis of the very valuable information that the commission should normally be able to provide us with after the hearings that it held throughout the country.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has enough experience in this House to know that the government does not control royal inquiry commissions and does not decide when they should submit their reports. We were placed before the fact that the session was coming to an end before we had received the report from the royal inquiry commission. What I am trying to explain to the hon. member is that the government is meeting its responsibilities by expressing its point of view while being careful to say that this is the policy of the government and that we are prepared to consider the opinions

of the opposition parties. The hon. member says that the country will pay for the commission. The country also pays him to sit in the House, but as we know the hon. member would have been the first to complain if the government had waited until November or December to bring in constitutional proposals. I seem to recall that the hon. member has been among those who have asked me most often to take a position in this regard and to submit proposals. Now that we have done so, of course, he is blaming us for having done precisely what he asked us to do.
