speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have just now heard the motion put forward by the Minister of Finance in respect to another closure. If there is any sense of outrage on the part of those people who are watching this proceeding, this must certainly fuel that sense. The fact of the matter is that we have now had one day in committee of the whole to consider this bill clause by clause. Within one hour's time of starting this consideration, the people on the other side supporting the government were yelling and screaming, "filibuster" and "time for closure." They did not even give us a chance to get our preliminary remarks out in connection with this bill and the Minister of Finance is now standing up at this point in time informing us of closure.
I know how much he hates committee of the whole and hates to answer questions. If members will recall, the last time we considered this piece of legislation the minister actually refused to answer questions. He sat in his place, he walked out of the chamber, and he refused to answer any questions. There were legitimate questions put to him in accordance with the ruling of the Chairman by people on this side of the House. He either did not know or was afraid to give the answers. It is no wonder-
Mr. Chairman, a question of privilege-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Minister of Finance on a question of privilege.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has stated something that is not true. I would like to answer the questions, but according to the ruling of the Chairman on clause 1 there is no obligation on me to reply to any of the questions. I would like to state very categorically that we have had a full day on clause 1 already, and not one single question has been asked of me. If the hon. member wishes to proceed clause by clause, I am waiting and eager. I have not imposed closure, but have given time allocation which means that there are three days available to discuss this bill.
After 19 days, Mr. Chairman, we have not finished clause 1 as yet, and any observer would realize what is going on. The opposition merely wishes to score some political points which they are losing because they are in bed with the PQ and they do not feel comfortable with it.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fact is that this is the kind of pathetic rhetoric the minister raises, ostensibly on a point of privilege, when he knows full well that he has absolutely nothing upon which to base his point. I take particular umbrage at the Minister of Finance questioning your ruling, because it was clear last week that clause 1 was an opportunity to discuss this particular legislation in a general way and an opportunity to obtain information fundamental to the bill. However, when we put the question to the minister dealing with his intentions with respect to the particular provisions of this bill, he refused to answer and left the chamber. We know how uncomfortable he is because he has no answers, and for him to come forward with the very boring response that we are somehow in bed with one person or another is an insult, not only to his leader in Quebec, but to every western provincial premier, most political observers, and the people in his own party. I would hope that he would at least desist from insulting his own colleagues in his own party if he insists on insulting the opposition.
At the close of proceedings last day, Mr. Chairman, I put a question to the minister's parliamentary secretary, as he was not there, in the hope that he would break new ground and perhaps answer a question. If the minister refuses to answer or is afraid to answer, then that is fine, but I pointed out that I thought it was a legitimate and fundamental question. The minister has brought in the ways and means motion, and he has tabled it at the last moment. They way in which he has handled this whole bill has been with a sense of incompetence, and one wonders how long he is going to be in this portfolio let alone an election, and whether or not the Prime Minister can tolerate having him refusing to answer questions on a very important bill.
There is provision in the amendments put forward under clause 13(b) of the ways and means motion which states:
-no interest be payable on the portion of any refund arising by virtue of such reduction.
Would the minister tell the House, in view of the contents of the bill, what the purpose is of having that particular provision in the ways and means motion?

Mr. Chairman, it was by way of reply to a ruling of the Chair that we amended the ways and means motion to have a similarity between it and clauses 30(a) and 30(b). It was done to ensure that the ways and means motion was in parity, if I may use that term, with the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: If my recollection is correct, Mr. Chairman, that particular aspect of it is not contained in the bill with respect to the interest division. I would ask him again if he can now tell us why that particular phrase was used in terms of the ways and means motion, as to why reference is made that "no interest be payable on the portion of any refund arising by virtue of such a reduction."

Mr. Chairman, according to clause 30(b) the refund will be $85, payable to the taxpayers of Quebec in compensation for the $186 million that was left on the table by

speechtext: The minister has now raised, in the course of his response, the fact that his government intends to pay back the $85 to the individual taxpayers in Quebec. I would ask him when it is the intention of his government to make that payment, having regard to the provision of the ways and means motion provision with respect to interest. Will this be an immediate payment, or is the minister intending to pay it in August so that there would be no suggestion, for example, that the minister would be so crass as to pay it out before an election campaign? Will the minister commit himself now as to when that money is going to be paid? It is a fundamental question, and I know that the minister would not want to be accused of playing petty, crass politics, but on the other hand perhaps he could give us an apolitical answer right now.

I must draw the Chair's attention to the fact that we have been discussing this matter for 19 or 20 days now; moreover, I think

that today is the twelfth or thirteenth day of debate on the bill and, believe it or not, Mr. Chairman, we have not dealt with one single question relating to clause 1. Hence, if the hon. member wishes to ask me questions on clause 1, it will be my pleasure to answer them and, in accordance with the desire of the committee, we shall listen to the comments of hon. members but I will answer precise questions only when I get to precise clauses.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister is completely wrong in two respects. First of all he is wrong about your ruling. We all understand that. Of course, the minister is not obliged to answer any questions and there is no way that you, as Chairman, can compel him to-not by bringing in the Sergeant at Arms or by using the mace-over his head, probably-to force him to answer questions. He refuses to answer any questions, so I can only draw the conclusion that he does not know anything. He does not understand the bill and he does not understand the motion so he brings in closure-he may call it time allocation-because he is quite uncomfortable here. He squirms in his seat and says we should wait until we get to clause 30 and then he will answer.
We are quite within our rights to ask questions. If the minister persists in not answering he will have to live with the reputation of being incompetent and unable to deal with them. The second point on which he has misled the House-probably unwittingly due to his lack of knowledge-is that he implies the world will stop if we do not pass this bill tomorrow or the day after. Anyone with an interest in budgetary matters recognizes this as a misstatement of fact. The budget tax cut and each and every piece of legislation set out in the terms of the budget can come into effect whether we pass them now, after another session of parliament, or even after an election. What we are trying to do in committee of the whole is to assist the minister so that he will not make any serious blunders. He cannot understand that.
We are trying to ask questions to bring out precisely what he intends to do so that he will not end up with egg on his face. If he is trying to suggest that these items have to be passed by tomorrow, he should remember that this government has developed the unfortunate practice of bringing down legislation arising out of a budget sometimes almost a year after the budget. We have just finished discussing a bill relating to the budget brought down on March 31, 1977. The minister should not try to impress his own people in Shawinigan with how knowledgeable he is.
I deal with one simple, fundamental proposition, and the Chairman has ruled that we can ask questions. He has implied by the fact that we can ask those questions that the minister, if he knew what he was about, should answer them. That is the interpretation we put on this ruling-not that he is not obliged to answer until we reach clause 30.
Will the minister tell the House when he intends to pay the $85 to the taxpayers in the province of Quebec? That is fundamental to this whole issue.
June 12, 1978
Clause 30.

speechtext: The hon. member for Welland understands this. He is an expert in financial matters and understands that the ways and means motion was changed by the minister at the last minute to cover up his ineptitude. I want to find out when the payment will be made out of the federal fund.

I have not put forward any amendment on clauses 30 and 30(6). If the hon. member reads the bill he will see that the payment will be made as soon as possible after the bill is passed.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I do not know why the minister cannot give us an indication-
As soon as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I do not hold myself up as an expert on government financing, but even I know that the provisions of the bill go forward. The effective dates go forward. If he does not know I will accept that, but let him say so now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I have to inform the hon. member that his time has expired, but I will allow the minister to answer the question.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote to the hon. member the decision of the Chairman on June 8 as reported at page 6193 of Hansard-.
-when considering clause 1 of the bill in committee of the whole, to allow members to express opinions or ask questions of a general nature.
I think the questions of the hon. member are of a very precise nature. I say if the bill is passed the government intends to proceed with the payments as soon as possible. We have to do the processing, and it is up to the Minister of National Revenue to make the final decision. "As soon as possible" is as soon as possible.
Dealing with clause 1, Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions. I should like a definition of "remote location" referred to in clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, it is the same as the decision we gave when we had the bill as the income tax bill, Bill C-ll, which we debated last fall. Incidentally, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Churchill because, after 19 days, at last we have a precise question on one clause, according to the rules.
The definition of remote location is as follows:
(ii) a location at which, by virtue of its remoteness from any established
community, the taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to establish and
maintain a self-contained domestic establishment,
Income Tax Act
Mr. Chairman, maybe I asked the first question, but I did not get the first answer I can tell you.
Oh, oh!
That is not a definition of a remote location. Is it north of the 52nd parallel or north of the 53rd parallel, or where is the remote location? I would like a definition of just where that applies.
West of Ottawa.

Does it apply to Churchill, or does it apply to some place in Newfoundland? Does it apply to somewhere in Ontario? I think we should have something definite, whether it is north of the 52nd parallel, the 53rd or the 60th, or wherever it is.

Mr. Chairman, it is not related to a zone in Canada, it is related to a locality. For example, there are some people who work quite south in the forests, I am thinking of my own area of Montmorency or north of Joliette, where they are staying in camps away from their houses. Also, there are those who work on ships. These people could be south of the Churchill area. If a person is in a ship travelling under the Canadian flag and covered by federal income taxes, and he is in the middle of an ocean, he cannot have a house. So the expenses paid for that person on board a ship qualify under this provision of the act. It is not in relation to any place in Canada, it is in relation to a location where a person cannot have a residence.

Mr. Chairman, that is still not too clear to me. If, for example, someone lived here in Ottawa and maintained a home and that person went to work at a site 60 miles out of Ottawa where he paid his own room and board, then he would qualify for a deduction on his income tax for, and it says here "not in excess of a reasonable amount". Does that mean that that person would qualify?

Mr. Chairman, if he is required to be away from his home to work for a certain period of time and he cannot expect to be moving back home and say his company is paying his room and board-for example if a person lives in Ottawa and goes to work for a construction company in Churchill, Manitoba, it will be quite remote. If the company pays room and board for that person, and he cannot be expected to establish his residence there, that person would qualify under the provision, as I understand it.

Mr. Chairman, it would pertain to anyone in Canada no matter where they are, as long as they are away from their main residence where they maintain a family? Whether that person is ten miles or five miles away from their main residence, they will qualify for this exemption and can claim his room and board. The confusion arose over the words "remote location". As stipulated by the federal government, remote location is a location where people would

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
receive isolation pay because they live in a remote location of Canada. 1 find that is confusing. Then this pertains to anyone who is not residing in his own home where his job takes him away. For example, if he lives in Ottawa and is working ten miles away or whatever the government may decide?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my description was a bit confusing. It is any area where there is no established community. It could be in the south or it could be in the north. As I was explaining earlier, it could be in some parts of Ontario where there is no established community. When I used the example of Churchill I was confused because Churchill is an established community. But if a person lives in Ottawa and goes to the bush to work in a camp at a site 60 or 80 miles from Ottawa, in the Gatineau for instance where there is no established community, that person will qualify.
If a person is working in an established community and away from home, that person will not qualify. By that I mean if a person goes from Ottawa to Montreal, or perhaps to North Bay, he will not qualify under the provision because Montreal and North Bay are established communities.

Mr. Chairman, what about a fairly large diamond drilling camp which may be located in the bush, does it qualify as an established community even though it could have been in that location for ten or 15 years? What would the definition be in that case?

Mr. Chairman, we passed a law. The interpretation is given by the Department of National Revenue. They look at the circumstances. If there is a site which has been at a location for a long time and the department comes to the conclusion it is no longer a remote area in that traditional sense, it could decide to disqualify those people who work there. I cannot be expected to forecast all the interpretations which the Minister of National Revenue will draw from the present act. What we mean by that is a location remote from an established community. If these camps are at remote sites and have been established ten or 15 years at the same place, one day the department will consider them in a sense as established communities.

Mr. Chairman, this particular section, a remote location, would apply to a diamond driller who might be working out in a remote area. It would probably apply to a prospector who is also away from his main residence. But how does it affect a trapper? I see in here where a person is away from home on a sort of temporary basis, and whereas trapping is not a full-time job, it is a seasonal job, then that trapper should be able to claim for board and room on his income tax when he is on his trap line away from his main residence. Is this correct?

Mr. Chairman, the deduction we are talking about in this bill at the moment-there are other deductions- is for an employee, and I do not know of any trapper who works for an employer. Usually a trapper is on his own and his expenses are deductible from his income.

Mr. Chairman, no, there are trappers who do hire helpers to go out with them. So these people, under this section, should qualify for a deduction if they are helpers. This would also apply to commercial fishermen who are fishing away from their own home. In many areas there is one licence issued and a fisherman could have five, six, or ten hired men. Those people will qualify for this board and room deduction, or are they able to claim it on their income tax?

Mr. Chairman, of course if they are employees and are working for an employer and the employer gives these people those benefits, I think those benefits could be exempt, if there is a relationship between the employer and employees-say between an owner of a ship and his employees, etc. In my judgment that would qualify. However, it is not the minister of finance who passes those judgments. It is up to the ministry of national revenue to make the final resolution if there is any problem.

Mr. Chairman, this is the problem we have. It is fine to sit here and say, yes, but somebody will give a different interpretation on this, or will give the final interpretation. However, for someone who is living in a remote part of the country and who possibly does not have the sophisticated media that we do here and who wants a clear definition of exactly where he stands, it is confusing. It says here:
a special work site at which the duty performed by him were of a temporary nature-
The temporary nature can mean that a trapper or a commercial fisherman can qualify because he is only there on a temporary basis to take the limit off of a particular lake and he is away from his residence. I take it that if he is a hired man, working as a commercial fisherman, then he could qualify because he pays room and board to the fellow who holds the licence. He would then qualify for the income tax reduction for room and board.

I do not think I have to add to what 1 have said. I think the hon. member can come to a conclusion. If there is a relation between employer and employees and they were working in remote sites, they would qualify.

This would also pertain to catswings, to freighthaulers who haul freight into remote areas of the north and are away from their residences for considerable periods of time in various parts of the country. These people are hired by the day or by the month as freight haulers. Would this also apply to trcuk haulers who haul freight over winter ice-roads into remote parts of Canada? I refer to the Northwest Territories, northern Manitoba, and so on.

If they receive free board and allowances for that, as far as the allowance is concerned, there is a relation between employer and employees. If they have to be located in remote sites, they would qualify according to the law.
June 12, 1978

This would also apply to railway workers. I would like it clarified whether it would apply to railway workers, Mr. Chairman. During the grain shipping season to Churchill, additional trains are put on. The workers are moved to remote locations along that 500 miles of rail. They may only be temporary employees of CN. Would they qualify for this?
If they have an allowance. If they are in a remote location and if there is a relation between employer and employees, they would qualify.

Seeing that we are discussing sales tax or a tax bill, not too long ago under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I recommended that the federal sales tax be taken off smoke detectors. We now see that smoke detectors will be required in all new dwellings under soon to be published revisions to the National Building Code. H. Brian Dickens, a National Research Council official, said so on Wednesday. Dickens, head of the Research Council's codes and standards group, building research division of the NRC, was speaking to about 150 delegates at the annual Canadian Building Officials Association convention in Winnipeg's Holiday Inn. Now that it will be compulsory under the National Building Code, is any consideration being given to removing the federal sales tax from smoke detection equipment?

Mr. Chairman, that is not related to the bill before the committee, but I can answer. There are all sorts of compulsory products in Canada on which there is some tax. I do not know whether a special case should be made in the case of safety by the use of smoke detectors.
In the construction of houses, and indeed in the construction of automobiles, there are many items which are compulsory and on which there is some sales tax. I find the principle unacceptable that everything which is compulsory by regulation should have the sales tax removed. That would be a bad principle to adopt. Even if one could make a special case because this is related to safety, there are all sorts of other instruments used for safety purposes on which there is a tax. If you exempt one, you would be bound to exempt the others. It is always difficult to pass judgment.

Mr. Chairman, the reason I raised this is because we were talking of remote locating. I am sure the minister will appreciate that the remote locations to which I am referring are in northern Canada, northern Manitoba in particular. There is no fire protection equipment on the Indian reserves and in the small communities. As this will be compulsory under the National Housing Code, and as these remote locations do not have any fire fighting protection whatsoever, I would appreciate if the minister would take this into consideration.
I will take notice of the hon. member's representation, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question on the same point of the tax concession for people working in remote areas.
Income Tax Act
I understand clearly from the remarks made by the hon. member for Churchill, and also the minister's remarks, that it would apply to lumber workers working in the bush away from their homes, and construction workers working away from their homes. What about the employees of tourist camps who work in fly-in camps, and room and board is provided by the employer in the normal way? Would they also qualify for this?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. If they receive allowances when they are in a remote location and there is a relation between employer and employees, they would qualify.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that vis-a-vis the sales tax issue the minister wants to answer questions very generally. I propose to ask him very general questions. Considering that the sales tax is within the provincial jurisdiction-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Which is not true.
The parliamentary secretary says "which is not true". The provinces would be very interested to know that a member of the federal government-
The Constitution. It is not a question of feeling.

I am talking about direct tax. I think the minister knows that. We have gone through a period of time which the minister says is a waste of time of parliament. It has also hurt national unity and wasted the time of the country.
Considering what I have alreay said, in preparing his budget why did the Minister of Finance not say to himself that he has a certain amount of money to distribute from coast to coast and, in relation to the population of each province, have a certain amount of money to cut sales tax according to their priorities? Once the minister started negotiating, before he presented the budget, it was obvious that he had to be flexible with British Columbia, Saskatchewan, the Atlantic provinces, and the others. Why did he enter into this area with such detailed proposals when, in the view of those on this side, he could have obtained the same result by saying we have a global amount of money, a certain amount to each province, within the general-
[Translation)
-as we say in French, by implementing the main features of our policy any province could choose to cut its sales tax according to its own priorities. Why not?

Mr. Chairman, I would like to answer that question, because I want to say again that during three weeks I had consultations with all finance ministers. We talked about that in October, that is a sales tax cut being, in the circumstances, the best incentive to stimulate our economy. We had talked about it in October, we had talked about it in January, and when time came for me to prepare a new budget, I did not want to do it without consulting all ministers of finance on that matter.

Not all of them.

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act

Not all? Yes, all! If the hon. member is suggesting that I did not consult Mr. Parizeau, I should like him to know that I consulted Mr. Parizeau and Mr. McKeough, from Ontario, more than anybody else. And during the three weeks the discussions lasted, everybody came up with suggestions and we made the necessary changes. I had an understanding with the other ministers of finance to the effect that on the day of the introduction of the budget, because I would be stuck with the traditional secret concerning the preparation of the budget, they were going to tell me either "yes" or "no". We considered then a possible sales tax cut. A number of them asked for flexibility and we made the necessary changes.
It had been agreed, however, because this consultation process was entirely new, that people would assume their responsibilities on the day of the introduction of the budget. Then, on the day I introduced the budget, following three weeks of consultations, I called everybody, having made the necessary changes to meet their requirements, and indicated to them the changes I had made, and they agreed. Never, during those three weeks, did Mr. Parizeau refer to selective cuts. No other finance minister was or would have been interested. [English]
I gave my word to all ministers of finance that I would call them the day of the budget. I did call them. Everyone accepted the responsibility, lived up to the gentlemen's agreement, said yes or no, except Mr. Parizeau who said, "I will give you an answer 48 hours later". The problem was this: it was too late, two days after the budget, to offer that deal to the others. Already British Columbia and Manitoba had put out their budgets. Otherwise, it would have been so easy.
What amazed me was this: at no time did the officials from Quebec make any reference to the question of the Constitution. I want to point out there is absolutely no problem involved here in terms of the Constitution. I spoke with the ministers of finance and said I wanted to help them cut provincial sales taxes and was ready to negotiate with them on the matter. They were completely free to tell me that they were not interested. But they all told me they were extremely happy that for the first time in Canadian history a federal Minister of Finance was willing to discuss his budget with them. I discussed not only the sales tax but monetary and fiscal policy. I tried to include them in the process. As I say, everyone left with the understanding we had to come to a solution the day of the budget. Mr. Parizeau did not.
He has done in his field what he wanted to do. I never tried to stop him. I simply said that if he did not comply with the national plan he would not qualify for the same total as the others.
As I say, we did not wish to penalize the people of Quebec because no agreement had been reached between the federal government and that province. If Mr. Parizeau or any other of the ministers had said to me before the budget that they would

not go along with my proposal, this issue would never have arisen. But I felt I had enough of a national program, and my plan was to offer to residents the possibility of an income tax deduction as I am proposing under 30(b). Nevertheless, that was not my favourite route. I would have preferred an agreement on sales tax.
I have done nothing to prevent any province from refusing the proposition. They were all completely free. Mr. Parizeau decided to cut his own tax the way he wanted to do so, just as two years ago Mr. McKeough decided to cut his own sales tax on automobiles for six months. But he paid for it from his own revenue sources. He did not come to me for money to pay for it. Mr. Parizeau has done it, but as there was no possibility of reaching agreement he qualified for only $40 million, leaving $180 million on the table inside the national plan. We have decided to compensate taxpayers in Quebec to the extent of $85 per taxpayer, and that is what we are doing in this bill.
What I would emphasize is this: never during the three weeks of negotiations did the Quebec minister of finance attempt to have his idea discussed with me or with the other ministers. It was only after we had closed the deal with everyone else, only after I had given my word to the other ministers, that he put me in an impossible situation after the fact. But even then I tried. I called three of the other ministers to learn if there was a possibility of agreement.
Too late!

Of course it was too late, because Mr. Parizeau had said no only after the agreement was in effect. Mr. Chairman, if I had made a special agreement with Quebec, after the others had signed, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi would have been the first to give me hell for pulling the wool over the eyes of the other ministers of finance. I acted in good faith, and they all acted in good faith with me. I cannot say that, unfortunately, about the Quebec minister of finance who did not say yes or no until the day of the budget. If he had said no earlier I would have announced I was compensating the people of that province through tax provisions.

It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say it was too late. It was too late because the fat was already in the fire. Supposing at the very beginning of the negotiations he had simply said; "Here is a certain sum of money depending on the formula used by each province to cut sales taxes according to your priorities," what would the difference have been? I am not griping about Ontario. Ontario did not object, but the proposal suited very well the needs of the automobile industry in that province. The minister had to make an adjustment for British Columbia and for Saskatchewan-

-did you argue the case before presenting the budget in the House? I can appreciate that you are Minister of Finance for all of Canada, but during your negotiations, did you really argue the case for Quebec, where secondary industry is not as
June 12, 1978

well planned as in Ontario, in textiles, furniture, footwear and clothing?

I ask the minister what would the difference have been in terms of general stimulation from coast to coast had the provinces been given greater freedom in this regard, had the minister said to them:

You can cut according to your own priorities, depending on what you did before. What is the difference?

Never in three weeks of negotiation did the Quebec government raise the possibility of select sales tax cuts. How could I express the desire of Quebec when Quebec itself had not chosen to express one? Selective sales tax cuts cause all kinds of difficulty. That is why it was desirable to have a national scheme. For example, what specific manufactured products would Saskatchewan turn to, to suit the best interests of their province, when they have no manufacturing industry at all? What about the position of the maritime provinces? If you follow that route, spending federal money just to favour local special interests, you run into problems. But on top of that-

This is the important point, never during the three weeks of negotiations did Quebec raise the problem of intrusion into a provincial field, never during those three weeks did Quebec mention the possibility of a selective tax cut, never did they tell me about it. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it was only at three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon that I was told that at six o'clock the same day, that is three hours later, Quebec would cut its sales tax as it saw fit. I told him: "At you own expense, much as Ontario did two years ago". There was no consultation on his part. I tried during three weeks to get information. The hon. member does not understand what is vital in that debate-
I treated the Quebec government knowing in the back of my mind that they were trying to destroy any federal scheme. That is their main objective, but I treated them like any normal provincial government which is dedicated to the best interest of its citizens. But, of course, at no time did they raise the question of a possible selective tax cut. When I called some ministers of finance afterwards, they all said it was too late for them and they could not agree to my making a special deal for Quebec.
That is what you are doing now.

No, I am not making any deal with the Quebec government. I am reducing the income tax of the Quebec residents-there is a big difference. The Quebec government has qualified for $40 million, that is all. What I am doing within my jurisdiction with the money left over from the
Income Tax Act
Quebec government is to reduce the income tax of the Quebec citizens.
And Quebec will collect it all back.

Perhaps so. I know they are in a hell of a mess financially and they will have to collect a lot of money in the next few years, no doubt, because of the way they operate things, because of the way they run the province, which is not in the best interests of the province, because of the crazy legislation they are putting forward which pushes thousands of people out of Quebec every year and which pushes investments out of Quebec, and because of the language legislation which creates a climate which will reduce the tax base of Quebeckers ever further. However, it is up to the Quebec people to decide in the next provincial election.
Quebec did not wish to participate in the national scheme but since they qualified partially under the program, I recognized that. Since the Quebec government wanted to have its own way outside of the national program and I did not wish to penalize the Quebec citizens, I have decided to give the money directly to them. Of course, Mr. Parizeau said in his letter that he will have to collect it back, and perhaps even more than that amount. 1 know that last year he had a deficit of $600 million, and this year he is forecasting a deficit of $1.2 billion. He has not forecast in his budget the $250 million which he will need perhaps for the nationalization of asbestos. I know he will have to raise taxes, but that is his own responsibility. The Quebec citizens will know that in the present federal budget we have put aside some money to reduce their taxes so as to stimulate the economy there. After I have sent the money to Quebeckers, if Mr. Parizeau decides to raise that amount of money or more, he is free to do so; but he will have to deal with the taxpayers in the next provincial election.

I would like to put a question to the Minister of Finance.
Did the minister figure out the expenses to pay out the rebate of the federal government directly to Quebec taxpayers paying federal taxes?

We have an organization called Revenue Canada which has thousands of employees who will have to do that work. Of course, that is going to cost money. It is difficult to measure that exactly because that will be additional work for the staff of the department. That brings me to the question that there is no tax collection agreement between the federal government and Quebec. I am very happy now that the government of Quebec should use the argument that because I am making that tax cut in Quebec they must go out and collect taxes and that is costing them about $150 million a year because they collect their personal income taxes instead of signing an agreement with the federal government which would cost them nothing. We collect income tax for Ontario, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Those provinces do not have a provincial department of revenue and we

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
collect their income taxes for them. It means only one form, one tax inspector for the citizen in Ontario or British Columbia but there have been two forms, two tax inspectors in Quebec since 1954 and, of course, that is costing them a lot more. That is what they called in 1954 an essential element of Quebec autonomy.
Recently, when I saw Mr. Parizeau he asked me to sign a collection agreement for him, that was really ridiculous. It was a complete denial of the policy established in Quebec by Mr. Maurice Duplessis. I am pretty sure that Maurice must have flipped over in his coffin because do not forget no other premier had dared ask such a thing of the government. But it is well known that we federalists in Quebec have been saying for a long time that it is a useless duplication of service and a pain in the backside for a large number of taxpayers to have to fill out two tax returns, to have two inspectors, to have two sets of books just because of that when it would be easier to have only one form every month for Quebec as for the other provinces. The federal government could send them the amount of money they have coming. But that is what they called in 1954 an essential element of Quebec autonomy. I do not have to make a judgment but I find that is costing them a lot for very little.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Red Deer has some questions to ask of the minister but he has a committee meeting to attend this evening. I am prepared to have him use my time now, and I will ask my questions later.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to seek advice on how the minister intends to handle the farm rollover situation; I believe it is under clause 14. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board suggested the other night that this would complete the required legislation so far as the family corporation rollover is concerned. I believe I am correct in saying that there is still an anomaly with regard to regulations concerning family corporations which is not covered in this piece of legislation. I would like the minister to tell the House whether he is prepared to bring in an amendment to it or whether he would expect an amendment from this side of the House.
The anomaly consists of the fact that farm property is not always included in the shares of the corporation. Sometimes the owner keeps the farm property outside the corporation and then the corporation rents the property. It is my understanding that this legislation and the legislation which was passed earlier do not provide for the rollover of the property to the next generation simply because it is not the farmer who is the operator of the property but the corporation, as soon as the corporation enters into an arrangement with the owner of the property either to lease it or rent it. There is an anomaly here which needs to be corrected, and I would like the advice of the minister on how it can be corrected if my assumption is correct.

The hon. member is talking about leasing land. If the owner wishes to do that, he can transfer the land to the corporation tax free before the rollover. That is the way in which the provision is understood by my officials, and there is no need for any change in the law.

I would like it firmly established so that the statement of the minister today will stand up in a court of law and will be understood by the Department of National Revenue, because at present accountants dealing with the Department of National Revenue find that this is not the case. If the statement of the minister will stand up in court and will be interpreted in this way by the Department of National Revenue, that is all I can expect, but certainly this should be a clear and established fact.

I have explained the law, Mr. Chairman. I understand what the intention is, but I cannot guarantee what a court will rule. We have a system for passing laws here. The text is there, and from what I can understand, it is somewhat irrelevant to the judge. He can read the text and conclude one way or another. I cannot guarantee what the courts will decide on any piece of legislation. A separation exists between the legislature and the judiciary in Canada. We read the laws as they are passed.
According to my understanding of the legislation, a person can transfer anything he has to his corporation, and from there on there is a rollover. He has to transfer it from his private ownership to his corporation ownership, and after that there is a rollover. There is no rollover if it is not transferred within the corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make this matter clear. Can a farmer who owns land that is being leased to a corporation which is the operator transfer that land without being subject to capital gains tax? Can it be sold or transferred to the corporation?

The questions asked by the hon. member are covered by the rollover provisions in the act. I feel I have been quite fair to the hon. member, but he is dealing with clause 14. It is difficult for my officials and I to follow the debate, if we are moving from one clause to the other. We are still on clause 1 and questions are of a general nature. I do not know when questions will be of a specific nature.

I thought I clarified my reason for adopting this approach earlier. If there is an anomaly, we are prepared to bring in an amendment. We would like to have our amendment ready by the time we reach consideration of that clause. If the minister will have his legal advisers look at that aspect before we reach consideration of that clause, fine and dandy. We cannot afford to allow this legislation to pass and leave any anomaly in existence. I raise this issue in order to expedite the matter and have it clarified. I hope the minister will have his legal advisers take a look at it to ensure that we are on

June 12, 1978

sound ground. Perhaps the hon. member for Moose Jaw will add to that, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, 1 am very interested in this particular clause. I realize it is clause 14, but before we reach that clause, I wonder if the officials of the minister's department could have a look at this aspect. At this point in time, if a farmer, who owns land and leases it to a corporation, transfers or sells that land to a corporation, that sale would be subject to capital gains tax because it is not being transferred to a son or daughter and he is not transferring shares. What the minister has said is not correct. I think his officials should look into this aspect so that when we arrive at clause 14 we can have a full discussion.

If a farmer is making a transfer to another entity, a third person, and not a corporation which he owns, he is required to pay capital gains. 1 was speaking about the transfer of lands to his own corporation. The transfer of farm lands has not been exempted completely from any capital gain. That is not what is meant. My officials are making notes of the hon. member's comments. They will read Hansard tomorrow and attempt to arrive at some clarification, if need be. As we have taken 19 days to reach clause 1, I do not know when we will reach clause 14.

There are a number of members on this side who are interested in this particular clause. I am referring to people who are involved in either the practice of law or have constituents who are farmers. The minister can expect a fairly lengthy discussion and a lot of questions on clause 14. If the minister will examine the record, he will find that government members have taken up almost as much time as opposition members.

A lot of government members are complaining because they have not had a chance to ask questions on clause 14. It is not only on the other side of the House that there is interest in that regard. The hon. member for Assiniboia constantly raised in caucus the problem of the transfer of family farms. A great deal of interest has been expressed both on this side as well as the other side of the House. As we do not have much time for clause by clause discussion, I know a lot of hon. members are very frustrated that we have not reached clause 14 or other clauses of real interest because of the filibuster by members of the Conservative party.

Perhaps the hon. member for Assiniboia has pressed this matter in caucus. If the hon. minister will examine the record from 1972 to the present time, he will find that members on this side have pressed for changes repeatedly, and that the changes which have taken place up to this time are a result of that pressure.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister should stop referring to the 19 days. Perhaps he should have a look at the number of hours his party has participated in the debate, as compared to hon. members on this side of the House.
Income Tax Act
Dealing with clause 1, particularly as it affects fishermen and employees of the coast guard who may be on assignment of sea duty, there are two particular aspects I wish to have clarified for the record. I agree with the minister when he says that it is not up to him to decide here and now how the law is going to be interpreted by the Minister of National Revenue. The officials of the Department of National Revenue have their own ways of interpreting, and I hope there are appeal procedures.
In the circumstances envisaged in clause 1, let us say a fisherman, a member of the coast guard service, or a public servant is at sea in Canada and receives an allowance for his food and lodging, and then is charged for that food and lodging. Would those be self-cancelling? Are they declarable as income, revenue or expenses? How are these envisaged under the provisions of that particular section?
If he receives an allowance for room and board on ship, according to the interpretation of the law and the changes provided, it will not be taxable income.

Mr. Chairman, that is in reply to the first part of my question. If his salary is adjusted and he is required to pay for his food while at sea working, for example, in a commercial fishing operation, may he deduct that as a legitimate expense on his income tax form?

Mr. Chairman, there is no special provision. If the owner of the ship charges him a certain amount of money for food and lodging while at sea, this is not a legitimate expense to be deducted from his income, aside from the S250 provided for in the act.
There is a $250 limit. Of course, this is an amendment simply and does not cover the $250?
It is a general provision that applies to everyone who is an employee, and it covers 3 per cent or up to $250.

It is basically an amendment under clause 1 and provides for the non-declarability of an allowance, the non-requirement of declaration of an allowance in respect of food and board only, and does not provide for an ability to deduct as a legitimate expense charges incurred for food and board?
I understand the interpretation of the hon. member is correct.

I want to get into a somewhat related matter. I understand that one is permitted under clause 1 to discuss general matters in the income tax field. This is very closely related to paragraph (1) and that part of the clause which appears at page 2 in relation to transportation charges. As I understand the reference to transportation charges here, a taxpayer would be allowed to deduct

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
reasonable costs of transportation to and from work. Perhaps I should establish that before I go on with my further inquiry.

Transportation in this area is similar to the allowance for room and board. It applies only if the transportation is provided to the taxpayer, or he receives an allowance for transportation. In that event the allowance is not taxable. We do not permit the taxpayer employee to deduct the cost of transportation incurred by himself. We simply do not tax an allowance, but we do not permit a deduction from income.

Perhaps it is not as closely related as I had thought to the matter I had in mind. In an earlier income tax provision there was an allowance made for a deduction by disabled people, or there was a refund when a person incurred expenses in the operation of their own vehicles. There was a provision through which such disabled persons could obtain a refund from tax to the extent of the cost of the gasoline.
I am wondering whether the minister would during these discussions entertain an amendment I would be prepared to draft in order to obtain a deduction or an allowance for persons who had to transport handicapped people. I have in mind those who transport these handicapped people for some distance, and under circumstances where the handicapped individual may be required to stay away from home for some period of time. I have a particular case in mind which I brought to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. It involves a child who unfortunately cannot obtain the necessary training in Victoria and has to travel to Vancouver on Monday morning and return on Friday night. This involves a cost to the family of that child of something in the order of $2,000 a year, in addition to the fee for the education of that handicapped individual.
Would the minister entertain an amendment during the discussion of this particular bill to cover a case of that sort? Would this be a legitimate deduction from income tax for those parents?

This is not related at all to employment at a special work site. The case the hon. member is referring to at the moment involves a problem. One has a lot of sympathy for the parents, but it is impossible under the Income Tax Act to cover all possible circumstances of this nature. I do not see how we could amend the Act to cover every such case. I am sure there are some circumstances that would not be covered where an individual might incur that type of expense in relation to a child. We have to think in terms of the general application of the law; we cannot provide in the act for specific circumstances.
With regard to the specific case referred to by the hon. member involving a disabled child who has to travel from Victoria to Vancouver for special training, my advisers tell me there is no possible way of drawing up an amendment that

would not lead to an absolutely uncontrollable situation. We cannot under the Income Tax Act look after all the individual circumstances, as painful or as difficult as those in the case mentioned by the hon. member may be.

I was using this provision for transportation as a vehicle for posing the question whether the minister would accept such an amendment. He has not actually said he would not, but rather that his officials would have difficulty in drawing one up. Would the minister entertain an amendment that I might draw and present in the course of this debate?

Mr. Chairman, this involves more than just difficulty on the part of my officials. I cannot under the present clause entertain an amendment which is completely unrelated to the act as it now stands. This situation is not provided for in the act and there is no room for an amendment under clause I to achieve the purposes of the hon. member.

The minister is aware of the difficulties of a private member in bringing forth an amemdment of this sort. Private members' bills really do not satisfy the need, and I felt this bill was a vehicle, being an amendment to the Income Tax Act, through which we could make such a change. This seemed to provide an ideal opportunity, particularly tailored to the bringing forth of such an amendment. Is the minister saying he would not entertain such an amendment if I were to bring it forward?
Under the rules of the House I could not entertain such an amendment during consideration of the present bill.

(ii) a location at which, by virtue of its remoteness from any established community, the taxpayer could not reasonably be expected to establish and maintain a self-contained domestic establishment,-

I presume that this type of change in the legislation would not benefit this person in any way. Am I correct?

According to the act, if the individual has to pay from his own pocket, those extra expenses are not deductible from his income. If on the other hand those extra expenditures are paid to him by his employer and if the occupation is of a temporary nature, he can qualify under the old act.

speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

On clause 2-
I wonder if the minister could give a brief explanation of what he is trying to accomplish in clause 2, Mr. Chairman, in addition to the headnote?

Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving technical amendment to the provisions of the act which deals with recapture on the disposal of depreciable business property such as buildings or machinery. When the proceeds on the sale of the property exceed its written down value for tax purposes on depreciated capital costs, the excess may give rise to a recovery of the depreciation claimed in previous years. This recovery or recapture is ordinarily required to be included in income.
Subsection 13, paragraph 4 of the act provides a roll-over. That is, the recapture is not taxable and the income is deferred to the extent that the proceeds on the sale of property are reinvested in a replacement property. At present the property qualifies as replacement property only if it acquired for the same use and for the same business as the former property.
This amendment broadens the test by qualifying a property acquired for a similar use in a similar business. As an example, the change will make it clear that the roll-over would apply where a cattle farmer sells his farm and moves to another location at which he intends to grow wheat and engage in other types of farming.
We have to provide this clarification because in the interpretation of the act by the Department of National Revenue they had a more restrictive interpretation of what we meant when we introduced the roll-over provision in the act last December.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 3-
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could give us a brief explanation of clause 3.

Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving technical amendment dealing with eligible capital property-that is, goodwill or agricultural quotas. The amendment is similar to that described in clause 2 dealing with the roll-over for depreciable property. When goodwill or other eligible capital properties are disposed of, part of the proceeds may be required to be included in income.

Income Tax Act
Subsection 14, subparagraph 6 of the act permits a taxpayer to defer or roll-over this amount to the extent that the proceeds are used to acquire similar replacement property. At present, a property qualifies as a replacement property only if it is acquired for the same use and is to be used in the same business as the former property.
This change broadens the test by qualifying a property that is acquired for similar use in a similar business.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-
Again, Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could give us an explanation of clause 4.

Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving amendment. Subsection 15, subparagraph (2) of the act is an anti-avoidance provision. It seeks to prevent funds of a corporation being extracted, tax-free, by shareholders in the guise of loans rather than dividends. This is accomplished by including the amount of such loan in the shareholders' income.
There are certain exceptions. For example, a share purchase loan-that is, a loan by a corporation to an employee to enable him to buy shares of the corporation-is not taxable. However, if the loan is made by one company to enable its employees to buy shares of a related company, technically the loan will not qualify for this exclusion. This is inappropriate. The amendment exempts the loans made to employees of one company in a corporate group to enable them to acquire shares of another company in the group. And, for example, an employee loan made by a subsidiary will be exempt if it is used to acquire shares of the parent company.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister could indicate how many corporations he anticipates will be caught with this new approach? When they bring in the affiliated company concept, how many have they anticipated they will catch?

Mr. Chairman, under this provision, companies are indeed freer to operate and can make a loan to employees who wish to buy stock in a corporation related to the parent corporation. Under the circumstances, I think this will facilitate the operations of companies making loans to their employees and will allow employees to buy stock in companies directly related to the corporation they work for. What is the exact figure? We do not know. This will merely simplify corporate operations, that is operations to allow employees to invest or take part in the operations of subsidiaries of the corporation which employs them.

Perhaps I could put my question another way, Mr. Chairman. When I ask how many are going to be caught, I am trying to solicit an answer to how many are being caught in a harmful way at the present time. We are familiar with the provision which allows a corporation to lend funds to an

employee to buy stock in the company itself, but how many are now being frustrated simply because this affiliate definition is not the law?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think 1 am in a position to give a precise answer. We have received representations to this effect and that is why we made the provision. As the provision did not exist before, it is impossible for us to know how many would benefit from it. We have received many representations on this, however, and we felt it was the right thing to do in order to make it easier for employees not only in a corporation itself but in its subsidiaries or related companies. It is impossible to tell how many people would have benefitted if the provision had been there before.
I wonder if the minister could indicate the significance of the date, March 31, 1977? Why is this only applicable after that date?

That is because amendments in the act last year made it possible to specify this date. Moreover, this provision also existed in the Macdonald budget, and the date set in the legislation passed last fall was precisely March 31, 1977.
I wonder if the minister would agree that what he is doing, in effect, is correcting a mistake made in the Macdonald federal budget of March 31, 1977?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is a mistake; I think it is a relieving measure. We introduced a good measure but we thought it could be a little bit better. We think we are quite good but we can always improve.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-
Mr. Chairman, this is a rather important clause. Perhaps the minister would be good enough to give us a fairly full explanation as to why the government feels this provision is desirable.

Mr. Chairman, yes, it is important and so I would like to read the explanation. Section 20 is one of the general sections of the act. It lists the various deductions which are allowed in the calculation of income from a business or from property. There are three changes to this section dealing with the new research allowance, interest on insurance policy loans and foreign taxes.
Paragraph 20(1 )(t) is strictly consequential. It has a reference to the new section 37.1 which is a special allowance for additional scientific research expenditures.
Subsection 20(2.1) deals with the interest paid on life insurance policy loans. This change does not alter the principle that such interest is either deductible by the policyholder or is
June 12, 1978

added to the cost of his policy. The change is essentially administrative. It simply requires the insured to verify, for those policyholders who want to claim the interest as a current deduction, that the interest has not been added to the adjusted cost base of the policy.
Subsection 20(12) provides relief for certain foreign income taxes. Under the existing act, the income taxes paid to a foreign government on business profits qualify for relief only if the income on which they are imposed has a foreign source. The existing relief takes the form of a foreign tax credit-that is, a deduction from the Canadian tax. The amendment permits a deduction in calculating income for any foreign income tax imposed on income that does not have a foreign source. Thus, for example, the portion of the foreign tax imposed on a consulting contract for a foreign customer only qualifies for relief now to the extent that the services are rendered outside Canada. The amendment will allow the portion of the foreign tax that relates to services performed in Canada to be deductible as an expense.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-

Mr. Chairman, I have some concerns as to how this clause relates to the Atlantic provinces, particularly in distribution of research and development across Canada and the interpretation of processes. We all know that companies are presently able to deduct all their current operating expenditures-that is, supplies, labour and their capital expenditures as well as new facilities, equipment and expenditures-from their income before calculation of taxes. This clause proposes that a company would also be allowed to deduct an additional 50 per cent of an increase in expenditure in research and development in the taxation year above the average for the three preceding years. This research is in addition to the eligibility of research and development expenditures for the investment tax credit which at present in the Atlantic provinces is 10 per cent.
I am told that total research and development expenditures in the Atlantic provinces in 1975 was $5.4 million. I am also told that no separate figures for the fishing and forestry industries are available, but the activities of these industries are such to involve little or no research and development. However, the government spends large amounts in these areas for research. For example, the fisheries and marine service of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment will spend an estimated $37.3 million in the fiscal year 1978-79.
I wonder if this is so and why we are not encouraging the people in the Atlantic provinces to take on the benefits of this new research and development incentive in clause 6. Before going on, perhaps the minister or his officials would be good enough to advise what the total research and development in Canada was in 1975 and compare it to the $5.4 million. If they are not prepared to give me the answer at this time, I would like to have it later.
I would also like to see how this clause will work. For example, if a firm spent nothing on research and development
Income Tax Act
during the last three years and in the first year of the budget decided to put $5,000 into research, it would, applying the 100 per cent straight write-off allowed at present, and now this 50 per cent proposed research and development write-off under this clause, total $7,500, being $5,000 plus half of the increase, $2,500. On the other hand, if a firm that spent an average of $4,000 during the past three years increases its research and development spending in the first year of the budget, it will get a total deduction of $5,500; that is, the $5,000 plus half the increase, $500.
To be eligible for the above allowances, in my opinion the expenditures have to conform to the definition of scientific research given in Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Act. Perhaps this definition is too narrow for the Atlantic provinces. For practical purposes, this regulation means the expenditures must be made either to develop new products or processes or to make improvements to existing products processes. For instance, on the east coast we are developing the 200-mile limit. If we in the Atlantic provinces are not taking advantage of this write-off, perhaps the minister could explain why industry is not taking advantage of the write-off. Is it because the definition of "processes" is not clear, that it relates only to manufacturing in the true sense in other parts of Canada? Or if a corporate fisherman owns a fishing boat with an estimated value on the books of $250,000 and he purchases new gear, would this qualify as a process?
I would like to leave that question with the minister and see if he could give an answer. There must be a reason why only $5.4 million was spent on Rand D in 1975 in comparison to the total, which I do not have at present. If the definition is too narrow for the Atlantic provinces to come under that clause, I feel there should perhaps be a widening of Regulation 2900 of the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the hon. member who is concerned about the level of research in the maritimes, as she indicated, of $5.4 million, that it is precisely the reason why, in the last two budgets, we decided to set up new mechanisms to encourage manufacturers and their operators to do more research and development.

It is because of the particular situation in the maritime provinces that we put the investment tax credit in Bill C-ll which I put forward in this House in December. We provided for the maritimes a tax credit double the national level, from 5 to 10 per cent, so that there is an investment tax credit for research and development much more favourable in the maritimes than in central Canada.
The hon. member asks why the definition of research and development does not seem to fit into the operation in the maritimes. I really do not know why. The research and development definition applies across the land. It is exactly the same definition whether it is British Columbia, Ontario, or Nova Scotia, an area for which the hon. member has particular concern.

Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that $5.4 million is approximately one-twelfth of the total industrial research and development across the country. In other words, if 10 per cent of the population is living in the Atlantic provinces in Canada and you have $5.4 million of R and D expenditure, I would like to know the total amount spent on research and development for the year 1975.

Mr. Chairman, I share the preoccupation of the hon. member. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I appreciate that is what the legislation says. I know of a certain individual who has begun a year's sabbatical from his employment to begin a new project. This is on his own initiative. He does not receive any assistance in what might be a very major development.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The minister has admitted he cannot help individuals.
