speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I have a final question for the minister, if I may. About five years ago the Economic Council of Canada recommended that the IRDIA graphs of Industry, Trade and Commerce be done away with. About one and a half or two years ago IRDIA was dissolved. Does the minister feel this measure he is now introducing fulfils the second half of the paragraph of the Economic Council of Canada wherein it said that IRDIA should be dissolved, but that there should be a compensating tax incentive to industry? Does the minister feel that this really meets that recommendation?
Yes, Mr. Chairman. We think that will fill the need according to the recommendation of the Economic Council.

Mr. Chairman, on Thursday evening last I had the opportunity of putting some concerns on the record relating to clause 6 of this bill. Can the minister give me some kind of explanation why he rejected the submissions of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and others from the business community and rejected the tax credit principle? I believe the Canadian Manufacturers' Association asked for 25 per cent rather than the additional 50 per cent allowance which was put in this clause.

Mr. Chairman, the main reason is that at the first ministers' meeting in Ottawa in February, it was agreed that there should be a joint effort of the provincial and federal levels. This is a system which involves both the federal and provincial treasuries. That is why we have chosen it, rather than an investment tax credit which would have fallen on the shoulders of the federal government only.

I do not know if the Minister of Finance or his staff have had a chance to read the rather carefully prepared comments I put on the record the other night. Surely he must realize this 15 per cent allowance is very unfair to the small business sector which, with its closeness to entrepreneurial ability, can lift itself into new categories of opportunities. Why was a more thorough examination of the small business interests not applied to the drafting of this clause of the bill?

Mr. Chairman, we have to segregate the question of research and development and the level of tax for small business. We provided a series of incentives for small business in the last budget and with the tax proposition I made some weeks ago to help small business. We must keep in mind that the level of taxation of a small business operating in Canada is very favourable compared to anywhere else. This proposal regarding research and development is in addition to it. We wanted to put all corporations on the same basis.

This is where I part company with the Minister of Finance. I thought I was very careful in putting on the record Thursday night how small business is discriminated against in this whole area of research and development.
June 12, 1978

Research costs small business in after tax terms much more than it costs large business working at the 42 per cent tax level. Did the remarks I placed on the record the other night fall on deaf ears? Has the Minister of State (Small Business) not discussed this lack of equity with the Minister of Finance?
Admittedly small business has a lower tax rate. Is the minister going to nullify that in the area of research and development? Small business is where the entrepreneurial talent is and where much of the opportunity comes from. Why give small business a much higher after tax cost than large business? I would like an answer to that question.

I cannot add to what I have said, Mr. Chairman. I appreciate that the hon. member is putting forward a good case. I explained earlier that we treat the tax system for small business more favourably than that of the big corporations. Research and development is a different problem, if I can call it that. As it is operated on the tax system, if you pay higher taxes you benefit more.
We have to keep in mind that small businesses are presently paying only half the rate of taxes paid by big businesses. The hon. member can make his argument but we have decided that rather than put the investment tax credit up to 25 per cent we would make this research allowance, because we wanted to make a joint effort with the provinces.

I am surprised the minister should adopt that attitude, particularly in light of the literature which the Minister of State (Small Business) has been showering on the small business community. I would remind him again that over 60 per cent of the working population in Canada is employed in the general area of small business. Government spokesmen pat themselves on the back and, indeed, other nations pat them on the back in recognition of the tax base they have afforded small business. I agree that this lower tax base has been very favourable for the small business community here, but in after tax dollar terms the minister is leaving this community with 59.38 cents cost on the dollar compared with 35.15 cents in the case of large businesses. There is a serious lack of equity here and the minister is neutralizing the tax benefit which has been put in place for the small business community.
If my remarks do not succeed in persuading the minister to change his mind, I honestly think he is making a mistake in refusing to consider certain aspects of this clause. Why not consider granting an option to small business enabling businessmen to take an immediate cash benefit in lieu of carrying the tax credit forward into future years? I know what I am speaking of because I have come through the world of small business and have spent an awful lot of money in my lifetime on research and development. I think there is a great deal we can do in this field for Canadian entrepreneurial talent in the development of new industries and spin-offs if we pay attention to this aspect. After all, that is where the entrepreneurial talent lies. This is where the big corporations come from-the development and putting into place of these ideas.
Income Tax Act

I can only repeat that many incentives have been given to small business. Of course, if one segregates one aspect of taxation from others, without taking the whole picture into account, one can conclude, for example, that the cost of research and development is higher for small business than for large corporations. But if one considers all aspects of taxation as they affect large and small businesses, I think we would all agree that small business has the better deal.
1 do not blame the hon. member for wanting more and 1 agree with him that small business is very important. That is why we have taken various steps to assist this sector of the economy. But since we cannot do everything at the same time in all directions, we have decided to proceed with research and development allowances in addition to the investment tax credit which was introduced last year up to 10 per cent, and also to introduce this 150 per cent write-off on the expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the Minister of State (Small Business) has been very weak in failing to negotiate more successfully with the Minister of Finance. I believe the government will be obliged to consider this matter again and correct a serious inequity which it is leaving in place.
I should like to ask the minister whether he does not believe that the eligibility for the tax credit should perhaps be restricted to Canadian-owned firms so as to prevent a leakage which has followed the placing of handsome sums of money to Canadian subsidiaries of multinational firms. Does he not believe that some of the leakage which has happened in the past could be prevented by restricting this tax credit to wholly-owned Canadian firms?

I think it would be difficult to make that sort of distinction. It would create all sorts of problems if we were to discriminate between Canadian-owned and foreign-owned corporations. I would point out that some foreign concerns have done very well in this field. Of course, we always hope that the gains achieved through Canadian operations will, first and foremost, benefit operations in Canada. Moreover, there is protection available under the Patent Act, and so on; the Patent Act covers the interest of Canada in research and development carried out in this country. To discriminate against foreign corporations as suggested could create all sorts of international difficulties for us.

So the minister is not taking any measures at all to prevent some of the leakage which has been experienced in the past when the benefit of research carried out in Canada and subsidized through tax remissions has gone to the United States or some other country. I question whether the minister should leave this type of situation wide open.

The hon. member is talking about leakage into the United States of information obtained from research and development in Canada. I would remind him that when the finance committee was in Washington the other day the union representatives there were complaining of the leakage of

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
research and development benefits into the Canadian economy, draining some jobs from the American system into Canada. So these things work both ways.
They were not complaining very loudly.
Perhaps not, but I want to point out to the hon. member that this is something which works both ways.

I am not aware of any leakage which is flowing north of the border. If the minister has any examples I would appreciate learning about them.
Could the minister explain why, in its approach to this subject, the government saw fit to kill off IRDIA which gave a better cost benefit to small business? Why take IRDIA out of the scheme when it was beginning to work so well?

One of the difficulties about this program was that it was too bureaucratic, in a sense. Under this arrangement, rather than make all sorts of applications and get into discussion with bureaucrats, the decisions will be made by the corporations themselves. I was President of Treasury Board when this decision was made and it was part of an effort to reduce the size of the federal administration.

Before I ever dreamt of standing here discussing these matters with the Minister of Finance, I had occasion to come to Ottawa in connection with this program and I did find the bureaucracy pretty rough; they wanted to double my true costs in the course of giving me some assistance. The result was, I could never afford it. But if one looks down the record I would be remiss if I did not remind the minister that the small business community is paying 59.38 cents cost on the dollar compared with 35.15 for large businesses.
I think I would be remiss if I did not remind him that under the 50 per cent additional tax credit he is leaving an after tax cost with a large firm of 35.15 cents on the research dollar, whereas under IRDIA the cost was 33 cents. I think he is going the wrong way if he wants to put an incentive in place. Let me come back to the small firm. With the 50 per cent additional allowance, you have an after tax cost with $1 of research of 59.38 cents, whereas under IRDIA you had a cost of 50 cents.
I think the program is not well prepared and planned and has not been studied properly. I think the government are going backwards in that area. In actual fact, they have gone back to a program which was recommended by Glassco in 1962, was studied in 1964 and rejected. We are now in 1978 and we need some new incentives in place. The minister should really give some serious consideration to an amendment before the bill is passed in committee stage and perhaps fix up some of the areas where there is no equity.
I realize I might be on the edge of the subject matter, Mr. Chairman, but I notice that the Minister of State for Science and Technology has come out with a package of research aid

amounting to $28 million. I realize that the Prime Minister has requested all departments to cut $500 million, and I wonder if the minister could tell us where he will find this $28 million in this soft buck shuffle.
Mr. Chairman, I did not catch the whole meaning of the question, but I will reply to it later.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to come back to my original point because I did not get an answer to it.
Nothing new.

Perhaps I should say that I got part of the answer. I have been told that $5.4 million was spent on research and development in 1975 in the Atlantic provinces. Considering that 10 per cent of the whole population of Canada live in the Atlantic provinces, can the minister say whether we are receiving and using this portion, and will we be able to use this portion in respect of the total research and development spent in 1975? In other words, what was the total? If we are not receiving the total, is it because Regulation 2100 of the Income Tax Act is too narrow to allow the Atlantic provinces to benefit from research and development?

Mr. Chairman, I think that because of the very nature of the industrial base in the maritimes we cannot expect their industry to use up their proportion, if I can use that expression, of research and development. Of course, since the base is very low in the maritimes the new system will apply to them earlier, because it will apply to many companies right away.
As 1 explained earlier, the investment tax credit in the maritimes is double that in Ontario, so I hope this will induce people in the maritimes to do more research and development.
If the hon. member wants my honest assessment of the situation, because of the industrial base in the maritimes I do not think that they will ever be able to use up their share of research and development. Research and development money will always be taken up in areas where industry is concentrated, and that is not the case in the maritimes.

Mr. Chairman, we have been told that the wording in the income tax changes suggested by the minister will help once again, as the Liberal government seems to like to help, the fat cats in the country, those who are in the high corporate income tax level. In turn, the smaller businessmen, who naturally have a much lower tax level, will not benefit from the deductibility to nearly the same extent as the fat cat, big corporations. Would the minister indicate, first, if this representation is true, and second, why he has not tried to bring better equity into the proposal?

Mr. Chairman, I think I have replied to the same question put by the hon. member's colleague, the hon. member for Capilano extensively. We have to make a distinction between the level of taxes paid by the big and small corporations and allowances for research and development, which are of a different nature. If you segregate just that, you
June 12, 1978

can come to the same conclusion as was reached by the hon. member for Capilano. But on the other side of the question, the level of taxes of the small corporations is half that of the big corporations. Lately we have made provision to ensure that small businesses will have more room to grow, and therefore small corporations' profit now is defined as being $150,000 a year up to $750,000 in accumulated gain.

The minister, as he is wont to do in these committee sessions, likes to avoid the issue when he does not feel it puts either the government or himself in a good light. Let me be specific. If a corporation increases its research and development by $300 in 1978 and its income tax is 48 per cent, what would be the total cost to that corporation of the $400 investment? Let us say they increased from $100 last year, which was their base year, to $400 in the current year, 1978, and their income tax is 48 per cent. What would be the net cost to that corporation of the $400 investement-the minister could throw in his tax credit too if he likes-and, second, what would be the cost to a corporation at the 20 per cent level? Could the minister give us those figures?
Mr. Chairman, I will have to ask my officials to figure that out and I will provide the answer later.

Mr. Chairman, that is a very simple bit of arithmetic. Surely the officials, with their high-powered computers sitting on the table, could come up with an answer relatively quickly. I will go through it again for them. Take $100 for the base year, which was last year for each company. Let us assume that they go from the $100 level to $400 expenditure for research and development in 1978. All I want to know is what will be the net cost to the corporation which is paying a 48 per cent income tax in 1978, and the net cost to a corporation paying a 20 per cent income tax; and, if you like, throw in the investment tax credit in each case.

We must make a distinction between a corporation in the maritimes, one in Quebec, one in Ontario, and what kind of corporation it is. I am entitled to ask my officials to make the calculation and give a precise answer to the hon. member.

I will make it a little easier for the minister. Let us say both corporations are in Ontario and both are in the manufacturing and processing business. If the minister needs any other help, 1 can even send him the answer; but first we will let him try to work it out to see what he comes up with.

This is an argument between myself and the hon. member. The hon. member for Capilano made the case earlier that if a larger corporation is involved in research and development, because of the 150 per cent provision and because they pay higher taxes, they will get a greater benefit. You cannot separate that from the system under which the small taxpayer pays 20 per cent income tax on his profit. We have recognized this principle when we go this route rather than by way of the investment tax credit. I considered that point with the hon. member's colleague some half hour ago.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, while the officials of the minister are making that calculation, perhaps I can deal with another question on the same clause. In its comments with regard to the minister's tax measures, specifically clause 6, CCH stated that it may be predicted that one of the effects of the new rules will be to cause taxpayers to bunch their scientific research expenditures so as to maximize the deduction. Given the 1975-1977 base of $100, for example, it will clearly benefit the taxpayer to expend nothing from 1978 to 1980 and $400 in 1981, giving him a deduction of $600 in that year, rather than to expend $100 in each of those years, giving him a total deduction of $400.
What is the department's reaction to the CCE1 comment? Clearly it would be undesirable to have a situation where those who might be investing in scientific and research ventures find it serves their purpose to delay any investment and to have zero investment for one or two years, because if it is bunched in in a later year they will receive a higher deduction as a result of the inept wording of this section.

In theory, this so-called bunching can happen, but it is unlikely. Some people can stop all research and development and start three years from now in theory, but that is unlikely. I do not think corporations operate that way. That case can be made in theory.
If one wants to cover all possibilities when drafting tax laws, a lot of complexity is added to a very complex system. We realized that there was a possibility of bunching research and development, but we did not think it was advisable to draft a system which would add complexity to something which is already extremely complex.

Having acknowledged that this loophole or weakness exists, why does the minister presume no one will take advantage of it? If we want to trigger research and development in our present economic state in the country, which does not have the real growth we want, and if this inadvertently causes any corporation to delay its research and development in anticipation of receiving a bigger tax deduction further down the road, surely that loophole is undesirable at the present time. Why does the minister feel confident that corporations will not take advantage of that bunching?

I do not think that will lead businessmen to close down their operations for three years and start again. They will take advantage of the new research incentives. They will not close down and fire their researchers and so on. I do not think they operate in that manner. They want to keep their personnel and keep them working. In theory it is possible, but it is not likely to happen.

Naively the minister assumes that there is no multinational corporate reality in this country. Has he not thought of the situation where research and development simply would be transferred to a parent company in the United States, allowing the Canadian company to have on-the-ground

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
activity, but with a view to routing the activity to Canada when it is able to receive its maximum deductibility?

We will monitor this situation. If there are some abuses, we can always cut back. There is no great incentive for any company to do that. I am glad the CCH expert suggested that possibility. We recognized it, but we could see no reason for making the law more complex than it is just in case this theory was put into practice.

Unfortunately, the theories of this minister have led this country into trouble. Once again through the want of a simple amendment, he will allow something to occur which perhaps will be to the disadvantage of all Canadians.
Has the government completed its arithmetic as to the relative impact of the deductibility on the basis of a 48 per cent taxpayer compared to a 20 per cent taxpayer?
Mr. Chairman, I do not have the answer. When I have it, I will be delighted to give it to the hon. member. There are still 43 minutes remaining.
Can we stand clause 6 for the time being, consider clause 7 and return to clause 6?
I have no objection to that. We can come back to clause 6, if need be.

On clause 7-

Mr. Chairman, as this is the first clause of many which have a bearing on the registered retirement savings plan program, can the minister give us an explanation of all registered retirement savings plan provisions which are in the bill before us?
[ Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I could always try to sum things up. As you know, we are proceeding in a rather complex fashion because we always have to refer to the section of the Income Tax Act that is being amended; trying to group all amendments into one would be rather complicated because of the many technicalities of the amendments, as I mentioned when I brought down the budget. I described that new system in my statement to the House on budget night, that is April 10. In short, we are providing more flexibility for those people who have assets and who want to cash in on them over a fairly long period when they retire; I think it would be better to proceed clause by clause. I could read each one of the technical clauses and by the time we have gone through the whole bill, hon. members will have had a complete description. It is very difficult for me to deal with all technical aspects at this point.
Mr. Chairman, if the minister wants to proceed in that manner, we will have to settle for that. Perhaps he could provide us with the technical explanation of clause 7, then.

With pleasure, Mr. Chairman. This is a technical amendment. It is consequential on the introduction of new provisions dealing with registered retirement income funds, RRIF, one of the alternatives to life annuities introduced for persons with registered retirement savings plans. Clause 40(2)(g) denies any deduction for certain capital losses. Under the existing act, no capital loss is allowed on a transfer of property by a taxpayer to a trust governed by a registered retirement savings plan, a deferred profit-sharing plan, an employee's profit-sharing plan or a registered home ownership savings plan. This amendment adds registered retirement income funds to the list of trusts for the purpose of this capital loss room. For the clarification of the committee, it is consequential to clause 35 of the bill, wherein we will deal with the substantive amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I received a letter from a constituent who feels the changes under this bill may not be altogether favourable. He indicated that he objected strenuously to the proposal to tax RRSP funds in a lump sum at death, or at latest a spouse's death. In part the letter reads:
The proposed changes eliminate the flexibility in tax options now available to those who may become entitled to RSP funds after a planholder's death.
I refer to such options as the right to purchase an income averaging annuity and the right of the recipient to pay income tax on the amount received, which is an advantage if the recipient is in a low income tax bracket. Could the minister clarify this?
Mr. Chairman, we at the table have not caught the meaning of the question of the hon. member and it could be useful if he were to repeat it.

I understand that my constituent feels the proposal to tax RRSP funds in a lump sum at death, or at latest on the spouse's death, is a change. In other words, has there been a change from the previous legislation that would create a tax on the death of the holder, or presumably on the death of his spouse? Is this a change?

It is my understanding, Mr. Chairman, that as far as RRSPs are concerned there is no change at all. We are here devising a new scheme that is called RRIF. If someone keeps the RRSP fund as actually defined, the situation is the same. He will not be affected by this legislation.

I would assume, then, there is an option to purchase an income averaging annuity, and a right for the recipient to pay income tax on the amount received in the event that the plan holder dies. I think that is what this person is looking at, a husband having the RRSP which has a value.
June 12, 1978

That person would like to know whether an income averaging annuity can be bought with the proceeds on the death, presumably, of the spouse.

There is a period of time within which the person who owns the RRSP can transfer it; that is, by buying a life annuity or opting for this new RRIF system. If he has not done that before the time he dies, then it is too late, as we understand it.
Is this a change from what was previously in effect?

No, it is exactly the same situation as was in effect. What we are proposing in RRIF is a new method for a person to transfer his RRSP. Before he could only buy a life annuity; now he can take advantage of this new fund from which he can draw on a regular basis and pay the tax at the level of the year in which he draws the proceeds of the RRIF.

Just on a point of clarification, let us say that the holder of an RRSP dies, and the amount of what is left in the fund is $10,000. The recipient of that would have to pay income tax as though it had been earned in one year. Is there no means by which the recipient could buy an annuity to spin-out the taxes?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know if the hon. member is referring to the RRIF and what is left to the beneficiary at the time of the death of the holder of the RRIF, and whether it can be passed on to his wife. If it is not going to his wife it is taxed at the level of taxes in the year of his death.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 8-
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister could again give us an explanation of clause 8 for the record.

Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving technical amendment. When a capital property is disposed of a capital gain may arise, one half of which falls to be included in income. Section 44(1) of the act permits a taxpayer to defer or rollover this amount in certain circumstances to the extent that the proceeds are reinvested in a replacement property. At present a property qualifies as a replacement if it is acquired for the same use, and, where the property was used in a business, for the same business as the former property.
This amendment broadens the test by qualifying a property acquired for a similar business. One example of the effect of the change will be to permit the roll-over where land used in one type of farming was sold and the proceeds reinvested in land to be used in a different kind of farming. This change is retroactive to cover property sold after March 31, 1977, the date when this special roll-over was introduced. I think the hon. member will understand that it is consequential to what I have described in respect of earlier clauses where we tried to broaden the interpretation of the roll-over provisions.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I have a question for the minister for further clarification of clause 8. He mentioned in reply to the hon. member opposite that it relates back to clause 2, and cited the case of farm land. Does this apply only to farm land, the sale of an acreage producing grain, let us say, where the proceeds are reinvested in acreage to be used for raising cattle? Or does it also apply to the sale, let us say, of a retail business, such as a shoe store, where the proceeds of that sale are reinvested in a clothing store or novelty store?

Yes, it applies not only to farming but to businesses as well. If you sell your business and you reinvest the money in a similar kind of operation, that is permissible. The problem arose earlier in respect of the definition of farming operation. The definition was too narrow, and if a farmer was operating a grain business there were some rulings by the Department of National Revenue that the reinvestment had to be in grain-producing land. We broadened the definition so that if a person sells a grain-producing farm and buys a new farm to raise cattle, or some other farming operation, that is allowed, rather than the narrow interpretation by National Revenue applying.

I would like to ask the minister whether there is any limit to the size of the operation we are considering in respect of this roll-over, particularly regarding business. How big might the company be that might qualify?
In the farming area the roll-over provision does not provide for any limit.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 9-

I presume the opposition will want me to give the technical explanation. This is a relieving technical amendment. It applies where a partnership has received the proceeds of a life insurance policy as a result of the death of the person insured. As the act is now written, a partnership that has received a policy loan will not be able to distribute the proceeds of the life insurance policy received as a result of the death of the insured without giving rise to a tax liability for its partners. The proposed amendment will provide for more equitable treatment by permitting such proceeds to be distributed at little or no tax cost, regardless of the existence of a policy loan.

Mr. Chairman, as this is the first of several clauses that deal with life insurance I was interested in getting that explanation from the minister. I would also like to know what it is that has changed in the definition of the adjusted cost base, and how this relates to the other provisions we are going to consider that deal with life insurance.

This amendment in clause 9 in respect of life insurance proceeds received by a partnership is just a clarification consequential upon Bill C-ll that was passed by the House in December. It is just a clarification to the act. There is nothing substantial in this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps we could have the usual explanation on clause 10.
Mr. Chairman, this particular amendment-
Mr. Chairman, a point of order. It might save time if the minister could deal with clauses 10, 11 and 12. They all refer to clause 35, and perhaps we could get them dealt with at one time.

On clause 10, Mr. Chairman, this is a technical amendment consequential on the introduction of the new provision relating to the registered retirement income fund, the so-called RRIF. Paragraph 54(c) defines the disposition of property for the purposes of capital gains provisions of the act. Ordinarily, a transfer of property where there is no change in its beneficial ownership is not considered to be a disposition; for example, a transfer of shares by a person to a trust under which he is the beneficiary. Elowever, an exception to this rule is made where the trust is not taxable, as in the case of RRSPs, IPSPs, EPSPs and RHOSPs. This amendment simply adds the reference to the RRIFs.
Going to clause 11, payment from an RRIF. This is a technical amendment and is consequential on the introduction of a registered retirement income fund as an alternative to life annuities for persons with registered retirement savings plans. Section 56 of the act is a general section that requires pension benefits and similar miscellaneous receipts to be included in income for tax purposes. This amendment requires payments out of a registered retirement income fund to be included in income when received.
Section 60, clause 12, deals with payments to RRSPs and from RRIFs. Section 60 of the act permits certain miscellaneous deductions in computing income. This amendment makes two technical changes which are consequential on the introduction of the registered retirement income fund as an alternative to life annuities for persons who have a registered retirement savings plan.

Mr. Chairman, on this general subject the minister received a letter from an executive of one of our life insurance companies and perhaps I could read into the record certain paragraphs and ask the minister to indicate what his reply was. The communication states:
The current law provides that the annuitant under an RRSP may purchase a life annuity with guaranteed payments not exceeding 15 years. In other words, for a 71-year-old, payments are guaranteed to age 86 and for life thereafter.
The budget proposals would allow two new options under which funds could be withdrawn in a systematic fashion amortized to age 90. I regret one aspect of these proposals in that they will create a new welfare class of 91-year-old survivors of exhausted RRSP funds, but that is not the main purpose of my letter.
It would appear to me that in order to be consistent with the new options, the existing one should be amended, eliminating the 15 year guarantee maximum and substituting a maximum allowable guaranteed period to age 90. This change

would allow a prospective annuitant to properly compare the value of a level payout to age 90 under one of the new proposals to a life annuity with payments guaranteed to age 90. As the proposals now stand, the latter option is not allowed.
Perhaps the minister could indicate the government's position on that.
Mr. Chairman, it has been extended in the bill, and I will give the hon. member the exact clause in a moment.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 11 and 12 agreed to.
On clause 13-
Perhaps we could have an explanation of this clause, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, this is a technical amendment. Subsection 69(6) of the act deals with dispositions of natural resource products to the federal and provincial governments, agents thereof and Crown corporations. The taxpayer who makes any such disposition must, under the present wording, include in his income the fair market value of the products so transferred. The change to subsection 69(6) restricts its application to dispositions made by virtue of an obligation imposed by statements or a contractual obligation substituted therefor. In this manner, normal commercial transactions are not interfered with.
In addition, another technical change eliminates "industrial" from the phrase "industrial minerals" used in these subsections. Both of these changes bring these subsections into conformity with the wording in other provisions of the act, in paragraphs 12(1 )(o) and 18(l)(m). The changes are applicable after April 10, 1978. This is to conform with the amendment passed in December, 1977, to make the situation consistent.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 14-

Mr. Chairman, before supper we had some discussion under clause 1 in connection with the roll-over of the family farm corporation, and in particular with the situation where a farmer did not transfer farm land to the family farm corporation. There are numerous reasons why he may not do so. For example, he may have done some estate planning and, having a large family and wishing to leave some of the land to other members who are not involved in farming, he therefore leases the land to the corporation.
The minister earlier stated that he could transfer to the corporation and then pass on the shares, but, as I say, there may be numerous reasons why he does not want to do so. The minister also suggested that if he did transfer the land to the corporation there would be no capital gains tax.
Over the supper hour I did some checking with a chartered accountant who does considerable family farm corporation work, and he advised me that there is, in fact, capital gains tax payable under certain circumstances. If the person transferring

June 12, 1978

the land is also a shareholder in the family farm corporation, there is no capital gains tax; but if there are other members of the family who are shareholders in the corporation, then there is a problem with capital gains plus other tax problems.
The matter could be solved fairly simply by bringing in an amendment which would provide a change in the regulation covering the roll-over of farm property. I am reading from the "Farmer's & Fisherman's Income Tax Guide, 1977", and the same regulations are found in the Canada Master Tax Guide:
A farmer can pass land on to his son or daughter or child, which includes grandchild, if the property was, immediately before death, used by the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse or any of his or her children.
In the past, in order to get around that provision, where the owner of the land leased it to a corporation accountants sometimes found it necessary to recommend to the farmer that he cancel the lease for a year and allow his son to operate the land or operate the land himself. He has then complied with this provision and is able to transfer the land by intra vires gift to a son or daughter.
I think the matter could be solved very simply by adding to that provision the following words:
-used by the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse or any of his or her children or by a family farm corporation, the shareholders of which one or more is a member of the particular class.
Would the minister consider bringing in such an amendment? It would solve many of the problems which exist with regard to a transfer, intra vires, from the parent to the children, which will now create problems with this new change regarding farm corporations.

Mr. Chairman, I will certainly look at the hon. member's proposition with sympathy but I think it is quite a complex problem. There could be many members in a corporation and not necessarily all the members are of the same family. I will study the proposition and report back. I am not in a position to agree to it at the moment because in all circumstances there is always a potential for abuse. Even with the best intentions we have to be careful.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that in this particular case there is any room for abuse. I hope the minister will talk to his officials and have them consider the matter overnight or within the next day or two with a view to bringing in an amendment. I cannot see, nor could the accountants I talked to, that there would be any abuse in bringing in such an amendment. It would be of assistance to many farmers in transferring farms to sons and daughters involved in family farm corporations.

As I said, Mr. Chairman, we are willing to entertain the possibility of change but I do not think it would be advisable to make such a change on the spot. This debate is a good occasion to receive such problems. It will be studied by my officials and if the representations of the hon. member lead to a fair amendment, we have a budget at least once a year, sometimes twice, so it could come back later on.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister what caused him to eliminate from the provisions of his budget, and therefore from this clause, the type of corporation that I might find in my riding-the ordinary small business in a city riding-when something of the sort was introduced less than six weeks later by the Minister of State (Small Business). Why were ordinary businesses not considered with farm businesses in this provision?

At the time of the budget we considered the possibility of incorporating the whole lot but decided to have a policy for small businesses. I did not want to spread it out with part in the budget and part in the package that was to come later. We saved it for the time when we were to make representation, where we could have a broader picture of small businesses. A bill has been tabled in the House and if we can deal with this bill quickly we will get back to the bill on small businesses.
Does the minister's answer mean that the incorporated farms being dealt with here are not considered to be small businesses?

Mr. Chairman, we considered farming a different type of business. The reason we make the distinction is that the farming community thinks it is completely different from the business community, in a sense, and we have received different representations. Of course, you could argue that some farmers now are really businessmen, but there is still the tradition that a farmer is a farmer and a businessman is a businessman. With the kind of money they make on some of the big farms in the west they do pretty well compared to many of us in parliament.
Mr. Chairman, 1 have a brief comment for the minister. First of all, I want to commend him for bringing in this provision in clause 14-
Who suggested it?

It was suggested by the Saskatchewan Liberal Association, by the Liberal party of Canada, by a number of Liberal members of parliament and by a number of members opposite, if the hon. member wants to know. The suggestion was certainly not confined to any one source.
I want to commend the minister for this and urge him to consider the proposal put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw. I think we are going quite some distance in making this amendment to include the incorporated farms in order to give relief from the capital gains tax measure. I hope the minister will look at this again overnight and see if it can be broadened.

Mr. Chairman, I wanted to ask the minister about a problem which is perhaps indirectly connected to the bill. A farmer retires, sells his farm and then buys an acreage near a city which was formerly raw land, not occupied or used for farming. Then he decides he wants to pass that along to his children. In effect, it is the same as passing on the assets of the
6324

June 12, 1978
Income Tax Act
farming operation he sold to the children, but at the moment that is impossible under the law; it has to be construed as a sale at fair market value and is taxed as such. He does not even have the right to set his own price if he wants to sell it to his children at lower than the market value. That is not acceptable to the tax department. Can the minister tell us why there is this Scrooge-like approach to the transfer of raw land, which is not necessarily farming land, within families?

The act provides for the transfer of a farm within a family. This is not to help people get around the tax law and make a buck out of speculation. What we want to do is preserve the family farm concept. If a farmer sells his farm and rolls the proceeds over in another farming operation, he would qualify for exemption; but if he rolls the money into a completely different business or into a piece of land that he will use eventually for speculative purposes, of course that is not a farming operation. If he rolls over his money into a farming operation, even if it is not exactly the same type-say he goes from grain to grazing cattle or pigs or whatever-as long as it is farming he will qualify for the exemption. If he rolls it over into something completely different he will not qualify.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister could explain the philosophy behind what he just said. Why should it be impossible for a parent to transfer property to children prior to death?

Mr. Chairman, we introduced the concept of capital gains in this country some years ago and eliminated the federal inheritance tax to compensate. It used to be that payments were made at the time of the transfer of money after death; now it is made at the time of the capital gain. Of course, if you have assets and transfer them to the children at death, you are not obliged to pay inheritance tax. But you do pay tax on the capital gain.

Mr. Chairman, judging from the exchange between the minister and various members, including one of his own supporters, there seems to be a possibility that the minister might consider an amendment to clause 14 to give effect to the recommendation of the hon. member from Moose Jaw. I wonder if the clause could stand and we could go on to clause 15 in the circumstances?

Mr. Chairman, I did not say I was entertaining the idea of an amendment at this stage. The situation is very complex although, of course, the hon. member tells me it is quite easy. We cannot just accept an amendment to the Income Tax Act without some study. I thank the member for raising the possibility of providing me with the information, but I do not think it will be possible in a matter of hours to draft an amendment and analyse all the consequences. I do not think we can operate that way.
Let it stand; we have the rest of the week.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister if the provisions of this section mean that shares in the family farm can be passed on through three generations without tax. In other words, could the tax be deferred anywhere from 60 to 100 years? Is that the effect of this provision?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, if the farm remains in the family. A father can transfer his farm under the roll-over provision with no capital gain to his children, who in turn can pass it to the next generation, as long as it is from father to son. subtopic: TRANSPORT-COAST GUARD BUILDING IN VICTORIA HARBOUR, B.C.
TRANSPORT-COAST GUARD BUILDING IN VICTORIA HARBOUR, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in the adjournment debate tonight because of the unsatisfactory nature of the reply given to me on Thursday last to a question concerning the coast guard building in Victoria, B.C. The minister's replies to my questioning were to the effect that, since a building permit had been obtained from the city, he saw no reason to change his decision. He also stressed somewhat the cost of providing a warehouse for the coast guard in Victoria.
Habour development in Victoria is of considerable interest to the city. The history is not common to other jurisdictions. In Victoria there is an Advisory Planning Commission composed
June 12, 1978

largely of elected officials, councillors, school board presidents and the like who consider zoning questions and make recommendations to the city council. This system alone was found to be unsatisfactory because it took account only of zoning regulations.
As a result, an advisory design panel was put in place to pay attention to the historical interests of Victoria and maintain the beauty of the city. This panel was composed mainly of architects and engineers who meet and pass judgment on the design of buildings submitted to them and decide if they are acceptable or not. In the six years or so during which this panel has been operating it is practically unheard of for any entrepreneur or contractor, including the provincial government, to put up a building which does not meet with the approval of the design panel.
Beautification of the harbour started some ten years ago and I particularly recall in this connection the case of an entrepreneur who wished to build, I think it was, a 25-storey hotel on the harbour shore. This would have been completely out of place and after a good deal of protest by civic officials and others it was decided not to grant a building permit and not to accept the building. The inevitable lawsuit followed, but the city was successful. A similar thing happened in connection with a proposal to put up another building of an equal magnitude. It has been accepted by everyone in Victoria that this is the only way in which to control the quality of the building which goes on.
In British Columbia they have what are known as design permit controlled areas-I do not know whether other provinces have them or not. In these areas the word of the design panel is law. The beauty and harmony of the surroundings is considered more important than the feelings of the entrepreneur concerned.
What happened in the case about which I questioned the minister was this: The federal government purchased some land from the Victoria Machinery depot for between $4 and $6 million and proposed to put up a building on that site. They knocked down some old shipyard buildings which were an eyesore anyway, and cleared the site. Then they built some docks and a shed to house a helicopter-I suppose it could be called a helicopter hangar. This is a concrete construction.
The minister made the case the other day that they had kept within the regulations for that zone, that the building does not exceed the height or the size permitted for the zone, but he was unable to make any progress with the advisory design panel. They have suggested several things to the department, all of them found unacceptable, it appears. The department is pulling its weight and insisting on building this metallic structure.
As was said the other day, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has a personality which would incite him to pave over Peggy's Cove to take a wrinkle out of the highway. This is what he is doing in Victoria. While the land owned by the Department of Transport does not fall within the design
Adjournment Debate
permit control area or the inner harbour, it is right next door to it, and it is in an area which the city and the provincial government are working hard to bring up to a higher standard, which we thought the federal government was doing. When they started working on this project, the Department of Public Works was in charge of it. They retained Willis, Cunliffe, Tait and Co., an engineering consultant firm, and Peterson and Lester architects.
Then there seemed to have been a falling out between the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works and, as it was expressed, they fired the Department of Public Works and turned over the work to their own coastguard with sole authority to proceed with the project without the architects. We now have the terrible result of a decision to put up a metallic building and to make no changes to the design so that it would blend in with the community. They have been told that a cement building would be more acceptable. In the matter of cost, the firm which sent in a tender for the concrete building quoted a price which was $17,000 lower than the tender for the other building.
I ask the minister to reconsider the decision and to see whether he could reopen the subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the hon. member's concern for preserving by all possible means the beauty of the City of Victoria, the more so because I had the pleasure of visiting there on two occasions for over two months, and it was the first Canadian city outside the village where I was born which I was visiting; I am therefore as concerned as he is in preserving the beauty of this really outstanding area of our country.
In order to respond more specifically to the hon. member's concern, I should like to convey to him the information I was able to obtain during the day. As the hon. member already knows, for the past few years the department had been considering to move the Victoria coast guard operation from the bridge on Johnson Street to a location which would not interfere with the activities on the bridge. With the support of the City of Victoria, the department has bought the former Victoria Machinery Depot property and made elaborate development plans for some port facilities, a helicopter hangar and landing area, as well as a building to accomodate administrative offices, a supply depot and workshops. The construction of the helicopter hangar and landing area is completed and has been approved by the coast guard. We expect that the supply depot will be available by December 1978, the workshops by April 1979, and the administrative offices by June 1979. The construction program for the base, including the landscape-garden, the landing to the port and the public parking area on the roof-top of the administrative building should hopefully be ready by August 1979.

Mr. Speaker, on May 15 I asked the minister if he could confirm the fact that there was evidence, or at the very least allegations, of four separate incidents of aircraft on final approach being greeted at four different runways across Canada with vehicles of one type or another being on the runways. In his reply, the minister indicated that he did not have that information available, he was unable to confirm it, and he implied that he would make inquiries in that regard.
On that basis, on June 8 1 asked him if he could now confirm the fact, at least in one case, the case of the Cran-brook airport, that the allegation had been confirmed, and that on or about April 20, within virtually two months of the fatal crash at Cranbrook, indeed there was another incident of a vehicle being on the runway while a Pacific Western 737 commercial jet liner was on final approach. As yet the minister has not confirmed that fact. Indeed I question whether he has bothered to make that inquiry.
When I indicated to the minister in a supplementary question that I felt he was shopping for another accident, and that he should address himself to this problem, he said that I was being unfair. As reported in Hansard, he said the following:
The hon. member is being unfair. He knows full well that the whole question of these communications is presently under investigation both as to the specific incident which occurred and at airports around the country. The inquiry is not related to one airport.
The fact remains that in February there was a fatal crash at Cranbrook which took 43 lives. The only thing unfair about my statement is that it is unfair to expect travellers to Cranbrook, expecting a very, very concerned group of individuals at the airport and an extended effort to control traffic on the runway other than aircraft, to find that simply does not prevail, and that the environment for another fatal accident is present. And a fatal accident could have occurred on April 20, had the weather conditions been similar to those back in February.
The minister indicated that he is concerned about these circumstances across Canada. Also he indicated that he is concerned about air safety. On May 15, he indicated that he

was very concerned about having and maintaining the high level of safety we have in Canada. That is simply not the fact and is far removed from the fact.
We have had this other incident in Cranbrook, yet the minister has not had the intestinal fortitude to examine that specific incident in light of the fact that just two months previously there was a fatal crash at that airport. He has not come forward in the House and indicated that he is prepared to look specifically at the obvious problem which is existent at Cranbrook.
The only unfair thing about my question is the fact that the minister seems to care little for the lives of the people flying into Cranbrook and other airports, for that matter, in Canada.
The minister also implied on May 15 and again on June 6 that all is well. Indeed, he said on May 15 that our total air navigational system, including such things as increases to our navigational aids and the like, take up a considerable portion of the federal budget. The navigational aids at Castlegar-and we have been waiting for months, for that which we have been promised for months, namely the replacement of existing navigational aids that have been described to me by one of the Ministry of Transport officials as more appropriately belonging in the Smithsonian Institute-are still there functioning. For how long will they function? There is a very serious problem in respect of getting spare parts for this ancient navigational aid system.
Today I asked the minister about fire safety. He touched upon this in his previous responses to me. The minister is reported in the press as having said that there is some concern. I really think this concern in the press is a concern as expressed in terms of the minister's attitude toward the Cranbrook crash and in terms of the minister's attitude toward air safety in Canada.
For example, the minister is referred to in an article appearing in the Vancouver Sun of May 26, which states in part:
For example, there is the inquest evidence that those-both inside and outside the ministry-who were concerned with handling Pacific Western Airlines Flight 314 on Feb. 11 did not take all care possible.
In light of the repetition about a vehicle being on the runway at Cranbrook, I would ask the minister to please examine specifically the ground-to-ground and ground-to-air control at Cranbrook. This has not been done, and in my view the minister is shirking a very serious responsibility.

On April 28, 1978, the Court convicted Mr. Treu on two counts, the first being that on or about March 29, 1974, having in his possession or control documents or information that he obtained or to which he had access as a person employed under a company who held a contract made on behalf of Her Majesty, namely Northern Electric Company Limited. Mr. Treu unlawfully retained said documents or information in his possession or control, when he had no right to do so, committing thereby an indictable offence, contrary to s 4(1 )(c) of the Official Secrets Act; and the second count being that after having unlawfully retained the said documents or information, the accused failed to take reasonable care of such documents or conducted himself in such a manner as to endanger the safety of such documents and information, again contrary to s 4(1)(</) of the Official Secrets Act. I would like to assure the accused as well as counsel that before rendering my judgment, I went over all the evidence-as I am bound to do by law and my oath of office, I went over all the evidence and exhibits and understood-I believe I understood-all the evidence presented as a whole, except of course for certain technical, very technical parts, which were beyond my knowledge-at least the part which required really specialized knowledge which only the accused and other experts possess. I do however feel that from a legal viewpoint-from the point of view of the law and the facts in this case-I fulfilled my oath of office to the best of my capabilities under the circumstances, after having gone over the facts and taken as much time as was required in the circumstances. I am clearly not saying this for personal reasons.
On the contrary, I am saying this to reassure the accused that, as required by my functions and oath of office, I went over all the evidence, and my judgment was based solely on such evidence and on nothing but the evidence presented in this Court at the trial. In addition, since I rendered my judgement, I spent the whole time between handing down the decision and your appearance today trying to think of
the sentence to impose, without of course preconceiving the arguments which would be presented in Court and without making a final decision, since I have no right to do so before hearing your counsel and the evidence they might present or before hearing the arguments of the Crown. I was however aware of the facts in the case and of the law, and it was my duty all the same to start to give the question mature thought and to think of a sentence which I could impose after having convicted you. As you see, neither my judgment nor my sentence are last-minute decisions, and I honestly feel that both are based solely on the facts, the evidence, the law and the precedents, after having-and I repeat-after having studied the file and heard the arguments of both your counsel, and this judgment and sentence are clearly rendered with a clear conscience and in accordance with the way in which I see the facts, law and precedents. I would like to say, Mr. Treu, that in my opinion your trial was fair and in keeping with the laws of Canada as they exist. The Official Secrets Act is obviously a Canadian law with which we are all bound to comply-myself, counsel, newspapers and journalists included. Moreoever, we are all, as citizens-and judges and people in high positions even more so-we are all bound by the laws of this country and I personally believe that the law is above men, above personalities, above all citizens, whether individual or corporate. You may not be aware of this but there is such a thing as contempt of Court in the presence of the Court and there is also contempt of Court outside the presence of the Court. The personalities involved are of absolutely no importance in my opinion. As I told you Mr. Treu, it is the law that must be respected; it is the law that is most important in our society and it is the only rempart that society has, that we all have. The last rampart that can really protect us is the law and respect of the Courts. I know that this has been said in much more elaborate and learned ways by a great many writers, scholars and jurists but the

fact remains that in very simple terms it seems to me that everyone understands that in the long run the only protection that every citizen has is the law and respect for the law and for the Courts. I come now to the actual sentencing. I do not need to tell you, Mr. Treu, that I have been working in criminal law for some time, whether as a judge or in other capacities, and I think that this is the part-it is often said but perhaps judges feel the need to say it more often because they are the ones that impose these sentences-there is no doubt that this is the most difficult part. It is relatively easy, even if it takes a great deal of work, it is relatively easy, because we have specialized legal knowledge, to study a record and analyse the evidence and end up by reaching certain legal conclusions and, after we have done everything, at least in human terms, with our knowledge, we feel we have performed our duty in the manner in which it should be performed. But when we come to the sentencing part, even if it is governed in the same way by the law and the precedent, the fact remains that the judge is a human being; it is exceedingly difficult for a human being to try another human being or to sentence him, if only because of this human part. That is a task that is almost humanly impossible, and I do not know any judges-and he would not be a good judge, moreover, and would not deserve to be on the bench, in my opinion-who derive any pleasure from sentencing one of their fellow men. That is exceedingly difficult. But this part cannot, of course, any more than the judgment, be based on feelings; the judge must rely solely on the law and on the precedent and on the facts, as well as on the criteria the appellate courts give us, and even then I think that the judge has no choice, whether for a very light sentence or for a harsher one the judge is bound by the law, and here again I think that this is the best protection. In your case it is even more difficult because your lawyers are right, you are an exceptional person, you are certainly not, in my opinion, a criminal; you have committed a criminal act but you are not what one would call an individual with a criminal career, far from it, you are a person who has had a most respectable life, who has great intellectual qualities, who as a human being is likeable, at least in my opinion, who has a family, who has children. You are not an individual-this makes it more complicated and makes sentencing more difficult in such cases. In your duties and in the onerous responsibilities you had you committed a criminal act, in my opinion, since I have found you guilty, but you are not, and I have never considered you to be, a criminal because I have never had any evidence of this, and I do not have any more, so in my opinion you are not one. I must try you, I must sentence you, taking into account, as mentioned this morning, the objective nature of crime, the protection of society, the setting of an example, deterrence and, of course, subjective factors as well: who committed this crime, your age, your personality, your family situation, your previous record-in this case there is none-your possible rehabilitation, your attitude at the time of the crime or immediately after the crime, your degree of premeditation and the circumstances surrounding the crime. Like any court I must weigh all these factors, at least I must select certain of these factors, certain criteria, and weigh them in some kind of balance, and this is what results in the sentence. In some case the rehabilitation factor is more important than in others; in other cases it is the protection of society; in other cases we must take into account personality, which has an even greater influence, which tips the scales in certain cases, with respect to the individual himself. Thus one must take into account both the objective and the subjective criteria, and after weighing, putting all this in the two pans of the balance, try to do justice to the accused in accordance with the law and precedents. And it is this part of course which should guide the judge, it is all these factors which should guide the judge in arriving at his sentence. I do not need to repeat myself, from the subjective point of view I have no doubt at all, Mr. Treu, that you are a respectable person in my view-you were, you still are-and I do not think, as I said, that you are a criminal. At a certain time you made this knowledge available to the government, within the framework of our security regulations, to perform a contract in which the security regulations were to be observed. In this respect you were in fact fortunate-to have all this knowledge-and this intellectual knowledge, this intellectual property that was made available to the company in the performance of a contract in which Canada had an interest-as I mentioned in my judgment-this intellectual knowledge and property
were to be observed and protected by security regulations established by the government, and the government-rightly or wrongly-is the absolute master where these security regulations are concerned. Of course the government receives its mandate from society, at least in the present state of the law, and if the government makes a mistake, well the law should be changed. However, within this very specific context, you had enormous, clear-cut responsibilities, and your intellectual property was to have been used within this very restricted context, and was surrendered to the government for good. Once the contract has been fulfilled-as I interpret it in any event-you were no longer entitled to keep these documents and either they were to be destroyed or you were to obtain permission to keep them. This was not done, and this is why I found you guilty and why from that point on the matter presented a danger to state security, at least as I saw it in the judgment. In Morrissette, the following is cited in the second paragraph, or at least on page 207:

"Deterrence is also an important factor. The problem is different if the purpose of a sentence is to deter the offender from repeating the offence, from that if the purpose is to deter others who may be inclined to commit the same offence, in neither case does it necessarily follow that a long sentence is required to achieve the purpose. Deterrence should be considered from an objective view, if the purpose is to deter others who may be inclined to commit the same offence. In such cases, the gravity of the offence, the incidence of the crime in the community, the harm caused by it either to the individual or the community and the public attitude toward it are some of the matters to be considered."
[ Translation]
So the deterrence factor-crime prevention-should definitely be considered objectively, if the goal is to prevent others from committing the same crime, others who could be inclined or have a tendency to commit the same crime in the same circumstances. In other words, the objective seriousness of the crime, the incidence of the crime in the commu-unity, the harm caused by it either to the individual or to the community and the public attitude toward it should be matters that could be considered. Of course, if the concept of deterrence is applied to the person who commits the crime, if the idea is to prevent him from committing the same crime again, we should pay more attention to the subjective factors, because if for example an individual had a tendency to commit robbery to prevent him from committing more robberies, we could in that case consider the subjective factor. In addition, if he does not tend to repeat his crime, we should consider his age and the subjective

factor would be more important than the objective factor. But where it is not a question of preventing another individual, or rather the accused, from committing the same crime, but rather of preventing other individuals in the same circumstances from being tempted to commit the same crime, in that case the objective factors must be considered. And I think that in your case in any event-I do not have the whole case in front of me, I have only a summary-but as I interpret it, and in any case, I feel that I must give more weight to the objective factor than to all the subjective criteria. In other words I must consider the deterence factor and that of setting a good example so that anyone in the same situation who would be required to have access to such important military documents, according to the evidence presented before me-this factor must take precedence over all the other factors, and I am referring solely to the evidence. And evidence was presented before me that these
were extremely important documents at least according to the expert evidence I heard.
